EAnswer recipes (one-glance)

UART code in 5 moves

  1. TMOD: Timer 1, mode 2.
  2. TH1 = 256 − 28800/baud.
  3. SCON = 0x50.
  4. TR1 = 1.
  5. Send: SBUF = c; while(!TI); TI = 0;

Any protocol in 4 moves

  1. Draw the bus and its wires.
  2. Draw the frame.
  3. Write the transfer steps in order.
  4. End with one reason tied to the question's device.

Any "you are designing" in 4 moves

  1. Underline nouns: they become blocks.
  2. Underline verbs: they become arrows or functions.
  3. Sort as Sensors, Processor, Communication, Actuators, Display.
  4. Label each interface and add a failure line.

Any thread code in 4 moves

  1. Find the tasks.
  2. Find what is shared.
  3. Map keywords to functions (table in each unit).
  4. Draw the timeline, then write the code.

3-hour plan

The FAT was 10 questions at 10 marks each, so about 18 minutes per question. Aim for 16 and keep 20 minutes to review. Each 5-mark part needs one diagram or table, 4–6 numbered points, and one line tied to the scenario's device.

They writeThey want

Your path through this unit

Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

    1Learn it, step by step

    Lesson 1

    Serial vs parallel, and what UART does

    In plain words

    Inside a chip, 8 bits move side by side on 8 wires (parallel). Between chips, that's too many wires, so we send the bits one after another down a single wire (serial). UART is the small hardware block that does this conversion at each end.

    Think of a conveyor belt: the sender unloads a box of 8 items onto the belt one at a time, and the receiver packs them into a box again.

    Write this in the exam
    • UART = Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter. It sends and receives data serially.
    • Two wires: Tx of one device connects to Rx of the other, with a common ground.
    • Data arrives in parallel from the data bus, is framed and sent serially, then converted back to parallel at the receiver.
    • One transmitter talks to one receiver. Slide maximum is 115200 baud.

    Remember: Tx crosses to Rx · parallel → serial → parallel.

    Check yourself: Why does Tx connect to Rx and not Tx to Tx?

    One device's output must feed the other's input. Two outputs joined together would just fight each other.

    Lesson 2

    The frame: how the receiver knows where a byte starts

    In plain words

    UART has no clock wire, so the receiver needs another way to know when a byte begins. The line sits high when idle. The sender pulls it low for one bit: the start bit, like saying "listen now". Then the data bits follow, lowest bit first, and finally a high stop bit.

    Both sides must agree on the speed beforehand. That agreed speed is the baud rate.

    Write this in the exam
    • Asynchronous: start and stop bits are used instead of a clock.
    • Frame: 1 start bit (low), 5–9 data bits (LSB first), 0 or 1 parity bit, 1–2 stop bits (high).
    • Both UARTs must work at the same baud rate.

    Remember: Idle high · start low · LSB first · stop high.

    Check yourself: How many bits does one 8N1 character take?

    10: 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop.

    Lesson 3

    8051 serial: SBUF, SCON and Timer 1

    In plain words

    The 8051 UART has three parts to remember. SBUF is where you put the byte to send or read the byte received. SCON is the settings register. Timer 1 is the metronome that sets the speed.

    When you write to SBUF, sending starts on its own. When it finishes, hardware raises the TI flag. You must clear TI yourself before the next byte. Receiving works the same way with RI.

    SM0SM1SM2RENTB8RB8TIRI
    01010000
    Write this in the exam
    • SCON = 0x50 gives mode 1 (8-bit UART, variable baud) with REN = 1.
    • Timer 1 in mode 2 (auto-reload): TMOD = 0x20.
    • Baud = (2^SMOD × Fosc) / (384 × (256 − TH1)). At 11.0592 MHz, SMOD = 0: Baud = 28800 / (256 − TH1).
    • For 9600: 256 − TH1 = 3, so TH1 = 0xFD. Then TR1 = 1.

    Remember: Write SBUF → wait TI → clear TI.

    Check yourself: What TH1 gives 4800 baud at 11.0592 MHz?

    28800/4800 = 6, so TH1 = 250 = 0xFA.

    Lesson 4

    Arduino Serial: the same idea, simpler names

    In plain words

    On Arduino, the library hides the registers. A 64-byte buffer holds incoming data, so the CPU can do other work meanwhile. Pins 0 and 1 are in use while Serial is active. If you need another port, SoftwareSerial makes one on other pins.

    Write this in the exam
    • Serial.begin(9600) sets the baud rate. Serial.available() returns the bytes waiting.
    • Serial.read() reads a byte. Serial.write() sends binary. Serial.println() prints text.
    • SoftwareSerial mySerial(10, 11); creates RX, TX on other pins. Max RX 57600 bps, and only one software port can receive at a time.

    Remember: Check available() before you read().

    Check yourself: Why can't you use pin 0 for an LED while using Serial?

    Pin 0 is the hardware RX line, so it's taken by the serial port.

    Final step

    Practice on paper

    Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.1.1, Scenario 6.1.2 as you would in the exam. Then do the 5 numericals. Then try your own numbers in the labs.

    2Memorise sheet

    • Asynchronous: no clock wire. Start and stop bits replace the clock.
    • 2 wires: Tx→Rx crossed, plus a common ground. 1 transmitter talks to 1 receiver.
    • Frame: 1 start (low), 5–9 data (LSB first), 0–1 parity, 1–2 stop (high). Idle line is high.
    • Baud must match on both ends. Slide maximum: 115200.
    • Flow: data bus (parallel) → Tx UART adds framing → serial on wire → Rx UART strips framing → parallel out.
    • 8051: SBUF holds data, SCON sets mode, Timer 1 mode 2 generates baud, TI/RI are done flags.
    • Arduino: the 64-byte buffer lets the CPU work on other tasks. Pins 0/1 are taken while Serial is in use.

    3Mnemonics & templates

    Template: 8051 UART: the same 4 init lines every time
    TMOD = 0x20;  // Timer 1, mode 2 (8-bit auto-reload)
TH1  = 0xFD;  // 9600 baud at 11.0592 MHz
SCON = 0x50;  // Mode 1, 8-bit UART, REN = 1
TR1  = 1;     // Start Timer 1
// send one char
SBUF = c; while (TI == 0); TI = 0;
    Init order
    Tall Tigers Sing Tunes = TMOD, TH1, SCON, TR1.
    SCON bits, bit 7 to bit 0
    Sam Met Sue, Ren Took Rob To Rio = SM0 SM1 SM2 REN TB8 RB8 TI RI.
    Frame order
    Sam Drinks Pepsi Slowly = Start, Data, Parity, Stop.
    Template: Baud formula

    Baud = (2^SMOD × Fosc) / (384 × (256 − TH1)). At 11.0592 MHz and SMOD = 0 it collapses to 28800 / (256 − TH1).

    6Numericals

    Numerical 1

    TH1 for 4800, 2400, 1200 baud at 11.0592 MHz (SMOD = 0)

    Solution

    Use TH1 = 256 − 28800/baud.

    Baud28800/baudTH1 decimalTH1 hex
    960032530xFD
    480062500xFA
    2400122440xF4
    1200242320xE8
    Numerical 2

    19200 baud at 11.0592 MHz

    Solution

    SMOD = 0 gives 28800/19200 = 1.5, which is not an integer, so it can't be done. Set SMOD = 1 (PCON |= 0x80). The constant doubles to 57600, and 57600/19200 = 3, so TH1 = 0xFD.

    Numerical 3

    Why not a 12 MHz crystal for 9600 baud?

    Solution

    Baud = 12 000 000 / (384 × (256 − TH1)) = 31250 / (256 − TH1). The nearest choice is TH1 = 253, giving 31250/3 = 10416.7 baud. Error = (10416.7 − 9600)/9600 = +8.5 %, which is too large for reliable sampling. 11.0592 MHz divides exactly, giving 0 % error.

    Numerical 4

    Time to send "VIT CHENNAI" as 8N1 at 9600

    Solution

    1 char = 1 start + 8 data + 1 stop = 10 bits. Char time = 10/9600 = 1.042 ms. 11 characters (the space counts) × 1.042 = 11.46 ms. Data efficiency = 8/10 = 80 %.

    Numerical 5

    Frame for 0x41 with even parity, 2 stop bits

    Solution

    0x41 = 0100 0001 has two 1s, so even parity P = 0. Line order: Start 0, then LSB first 1 0 0 0 0 0 1 0, then P 0, then stop 1 1. Total 12 bits, efficiency 8/12 = 66.7 %.

    7Solved PYQ scenarios

    Scenario 6.1.1PYQ Q610 marks

    Continuous "VIT CHENNAI" over UART

    (a) Design an Embedded C program for the 8051 to transmit "VIT CHENNAI" via UART at 9600 baud, continuously, with 1 s between transmissions. Crystal 11.0592 MHz. 5 M (b) Explain the role of SCON and how Timer 1 generates the baud rate. 5 M

    Solution
    Decode the question: "9600 + 11.0592" → TH1=0xFD. "continuous" → while(1). "delay of 1 second" → Timer 0, because Timer 1 is busy making baud. "string" → pointer loop.

    (a) Program 5M

    #include <reg51.h>
void uart_init(void) {
  TMOD = 0x21;   // T1 mode 2 (baud), T0 mode 1 (delay)
  TH1  = 0xFD;   // 9600 baud
  SCON = 0x50;   // mode 1, 8-bit, REN = 1
  TR1  = 1;
}
void send_char(char c) {
  SBUF = c;
  while (TI == 0);
  TI = 0;
}
void send_string(const char *s) {
  while (*s) send_char(*s++);
}
void delay_1s(void) {
  unsigned char i;
  for (i = 0; i < 20; i++) {   // 20 x 50 ms
    TH0 = 0x4C; TL0 = 0x00;    // 65536 - 46080 = 19456
    TR0 = 1;
    while (TF0 == 0);
    TR0 = 0; TF0 = 0;
  }
}
void main(void) {
  uart_init();
  while (1) {
    send_string("VIT CHENNAI");
    delay_1s();
  }
}

    Delay working: machine cycle = 12/11.0592 MHz = 1.085 µs. 50 ms / 1.085 µs = 46080 counts.

    (b) SCON 3M It is the serial control register at 98H.

    SM0SM1SM2RENTB8RB8TIRI
    01010000

    SM0 SM1 = 01 selects mode 1 (8-bit UART, variable baud). REN = 1 enables reception. TI is set when a byte finishes sending, RI when one arrives. Software must clear both. Result: SCON = 0x50.

    Timer 1 2M Mode 2 auto-reloads TH1 into TL1 on each overflow, so the rate needs no software. Baud = 28800/(256 − TH1). For 9600, 256 − TH1 = 3, so TH1 = 253 = 0xFD. Set TR1 = 1 to start.

    Scenario 6.1.2Built like your FAT10 marks

    Sensor logger sends to a PC, receives commands

    A greenhouse 8051 sends one temperature byte to a PC every cycle at 4800 baud and must switch a fan on P2.0 when the PC sends 'F'. (a) Draw the frame and give the full setup. 4 M (b) Write the code. 4 M (c) Why is the serial interrupt better here? 2 M

    Solution

    (a) 4M Frame: Start, 8 data LSB first, Stop (10 bits). Setup: TMOD=0x20; TH1=0xFA; SCON=0x50; TR1=1; since 28800/4800 = 6 and 256 − 6 = 250 = 0xFA.

    (b) 4M

    #include <reg51.h>
sbit FAN = P2^0;
extern unsigned char read_temp(void);
volatile bit tx_done = 1;
void serial_isr(void) interrupt 4 {
  if (RI) { RI = 0; FAN = (SBUF == 'F'); }
  if (TI) { TI = 0; tx_done = 1; }
}
void main(void) {
  TMOD=0x20; TH1=0xFA; SCON=0x50; TR1=1;
  EA = 1; ES = 1;
  while (1) {
    while (!tx_done);      // previous byte finished
    tx_done = 0;
    SBUF = read_temp();
  }
}

    (c) 2M Polling RI could miss the 'F' while the CPU is busy reading the sensor. An interrupt responds as soon as the byte lands, and the CPU is free in between.

    8Tips & traps

    Trap: Timer 1 can't also make your 1 s delay. It's occupied by baud generation, so use Timer 0 and TMOD=0x21.
    Tip: Always write "Assume SMOD = 0" and show 28800/(256 − TH1). That working earns marks even if the final hex slips.
    Trap: The space in a string is a character. "VIT CHENNAI" is 11 characters, not 10.
    MODULE 6 · UNIT 2

    RS-232

    The old standard that defines what serial signals look like on a cable.

    TheoryPin tableHandshake
    How it comes in the exam

    This is a short theory deck, so expect it as a part-question or as a comparison with UART: "pins, handshaking, DTE vs DCE, why USB replaced it".

    Your path through this unit

    Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

      1Learn it, step by step

      Lesson 1

      What RS-232 is, and how it differs from UART

      In plain words

      UART decides *which bits* to send. RS-232 is the agreement about *how those bits look on a cable*: voltage levels, timing and which pin does what. It's like the difference between a letter's content and the postal rules for the envelope.

      Write this in the exam
      • RS-232 = Recommended Standard 232, an interface standard commonly used in computer serial ports.
      • Defines the electrical characteristics and timing of signals.
      • Introduced in 1962, C revision in 1969, current version TIA-232-F (1997).
      • Supports both synchronous and asynchronous transmission.

      Remember: UART frames the bits · RS-232 defines the cable.

      Check yourself: Does RS-232 define the start and stop bits?

      No, that's the UART's job. RS-232 defines the electrical signal and connector.

      Lesson 2

      DTE, DCE and the DB-9 connector

      In plain words

      RS-232 gives each device one of two roles so that everyone agrees who transmits on which pin. DTE is the "computer" side. DCE is the "communication equipment" side, like a modem.

      Write this in the exam
      • DTE: terminals and computers that send and receive data.
      • DCE: communication equipment, such as modems, responsible for transferring data.
      • DB-9: 1 DCD, 2 RxD, 3 TxD, 4 DTR, 5 GND, 6 DSR, 7 RTS, 8 CTS, 9 RI.

      Remember: DTE = computer · DCE = modem.

      Check yourself: Which pin number is signal ground on a DB-9?

      Pin 5.

      Lesson 3

      Handshaking and why USB replaced it

      In plain words

      Handshaking is two devices checking with each other before talking, like "Are you there?", "Yes", "Can I send?", "Go ahead". If the receiver's buffer fills, it withdraws permission and the sender pauses, so nothing is lost.

      Write this in the exam
      • Handshaking pins: DTR, DSR, RTS, CTS, DCD, RI. They coordinate the transfer for fast, reliable transmission.
      • Limitations: limited speed, relatively large voltage swing, large standard connectors. These motivated USB.
      • Multi-drop connection among more than two devices is not defined.

      Remember: Ready pair (DTR/DSR), then permission pair (RTS/CTS).

      Check yourself: Which signal does a modem drop to pause the computer?

      CTS (Clear To Send).

      Final step

      Practice on paper

      Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.2.1, Scenario 6.2.2 as you would in the exam.

      2Memorise sheet

      • RS-232 = Recommended Standard 232. An interface standard for computer serial ports.
      • It defines electrical characteristics and timing of signals.
      • Introduced 1962, C revision 1969, current version TIA-232-F (1997).
      • Data goes as a time series of bits. It supports both synchronous and asynchronous modes.
      • DTE = terminals and computers that send/receive data. DCE = communication equipment such as modems.
      • Limits: limited speed, large voltage swing, large connectors, and multi-drop between more than two devices not defined. These led to USB.
      • Handshake pins: DTR, DSR, RTS, CTS, DCD, RI.

      3Mnemonics & templates

      DB-9 pins 1 to 9
      Dad Reads Tiny Dull Grammar, Don't Read Comics Regularly = DCD, RxD, TxD, DTR, GND, DSR, RTS, CTS, RI.
      Template: Handshake story, 3 marks

      DTE raises DTR ("I'm ready") → DCE raises DSR ("me too") → DTE raises RTS ("may I send?") → DCE raises CTS ("go") → data flows on TxD/RxD. DCD reports a carrier and RI reports an incoming ring.

      6Solved scenarios

      Scenario 6.2.1Built like your FAT10 marks

      Connecting a lab instrument to a modem

      A legacy lab instrument (computer side) sends readings to a remote centre through a modem over RS-232. (a) Classify each device and draw the DB-9 connection. 4 M (b) Explain how the handshake prevents data loss. 4 M (c) State two limitations and what replaced it. 2 M

      Solution

      (a) 4M Instrument = DTE, modem = DCE. Straight-through cable: pin 2 RxD, 3 TxD, 4 DTR, 5 GND, 6 DSR, 7 RTS, 8 CTS, with 1 DCD and 9 RI driven by the modem.

      (b) 4M Data transfer must be coordinated. The instrument raises DTR and the modem answers with DSR to confirm both are powered and ready. The instrument raises RTS when it has data. The modem raises CTS only when its buffer can accept data. If the modem's buffer fills it drops CTS, so the instrument pauses. Nothing is overwritten, so no bytes are lost.

      (c) 2M Limited speed with a large voltage swing and bulky connectors. Multi-drop between more than two devices isn't defined. USB displaced it.

      Scenario 6.2.2Built like your FAT10 marks

      UART vs RS-232 in an 8051 to PC link

      An engineer says "RS-232 and UART are the same thing". (a) Correct this statement. 4 M (b) Design the 8051 to PC link with a block diagram. 4 M (c) State what each RS-232 standard element specifies. 2 M

      Solution

      (a) 4M UART is a hardware block that frames bytes: start, data, parity, stop. RS-232 is an interface standard that defines electrical characteristics, timing and connector signals. UART decides *what bits* go out. RS-232 decides *how they look on the cable*. A UART commonly sits behind an RS-232 driver.

      (b) 4M

      Configure the 8051 for mode 1 at 9600 baud. Connect TX, RX and common GND. Hardware handshake lines are optional.

      (c) 2M Voltage levels and timing (electrical), plus each pin's signal function such as TxD, RxD and the handshake lines (functional).

      7Tips & traps

      Trap: The level-shifter (MAX232) isn't in your slides, but it earns a design mark. Never wire 8051 TTL directly to an RS-232 port.
      Tip: Write the pin table with the mnemonic. A 9-row table is a quick, safe 3 marks.
      MODULE 6 · UNIT 3

      SPI

      Four wires, a clock from the master, and very high speed on the board.

      Theory + numericalsCompare with I²C
      How it comes in the exam

      Your paper didn't have a dedicated SPI question, but SPI is the natural partner to the I²C scenario. Expect "choose SPI or I²C", "connect N slaves", or a data-rate calculation.

      Your path through this unit

      Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

        1Learn it, step by step

        Lesson 1

        The four wires and the shift-register ring

        In plain words

        Picture two people passing beads around a circle. Each time a clock ticks, one bead moves from the master to the slave and one moves from the slave to the master. After 8 ticks they have swapped a full byte. That circle of two shift registers is SPI, and it's why SPI is naturally full duplex.

        Write this in the exam
        • SPI = Serial Peripheral Interface: full-duplex, synchronous, high speed, short distance.
        • MOSI: master generates data, slave receives. MISO: slave generates data, master receives.
        • SCLK: clock generated by the master. SS/CS: master selects a particular slave.
        • Slide spec: 4 wires, 10 Mbps, 1 master, theoretically unlimited slaves.

        Remember: One clock = one bit each way.

        Check yourself: Who generates the clock in SPI?

        Always the master.

        Lesson 2

        A transfer step by step, and clock modes

        In plain words

        Slave Select is active low: it rests high, and pulling it low is like tapping one person on the shoulder. CPOL says whether the clock rests low or high. CPHA says which edge is used for reading. Master and slave must match, otherwise they read at the wrong moments.

        Write this in the exam
        • Step 1: master outputs the clock. Step 2: master pulls SS low. Step 3: master sends on MOSI one bit at a time. Step 4: slave responds on MISO.
        • Mode 0 (CPOL 0, CPHA 0), Mode 1 (0,1), Mode 2 (1,0), Mode 3 (1,1).
        • Only one bit is transmitted per clock, so clock frequency sets the data rate.

        Remember: SS low means "you're chosen".

        Check yourself: In mode 2, what's the clock level when idle?

        High, since CPOL = 1.

        Lesson 3

        Connecting many slaves

        In plain words

        Two options. Independent gives each slave its own select line, so the master can talk to any one directly but uses more pins. Daisy chain shares one select line, and data ripples through every slave like a bucket line, saving pins but taking more clocks.

        Write this in the exam
        • Independent: dedicated select per slave. Master pins = 3 + N.
        • Daisy chain: single select. Master MOSI → S1 MOSI, S1 MISO → S2 MOSI, last MISO → master MISO.

        Remember: Pins short? Daisy chain.

        Check yourself: Three independent slaves need how many master pins?

        MOSI + MISO + SCLK + 3 SS = 6.

        Lesson 4

        Advantages, disadvantages, Arduino calls

        In plain words

        SPI's strength is simplicity and speed. Its weakness is that there's no confirmation the data arrived, and every extra device costs wires.

        Write this in the exam
        • Advantages: full duplex, high speed, not limited to 8 bits, slave needs no oscillator, no start/stop bits, no conflict since the master controls.
        • Disadvantages: four pins, single master, dedicated SS per slave, no acknowledgement, device-based speed.
        • Applications: SD card, EEPROM, Flash, ADC, audio codec, LCD, touchscreen.
        • Arduino: SPI.begin(), SPI.setClockDivider(), SPI.setDataMode(), SPI.transfer(val).

        Remember: SPI's two weak points: no ACK, one SS each.

        Check yourself: Name a device best suited to SPI and say why.

        An SD card, because it moves large blocks and benefits from SPI's speed.

        Final step

        Practice on paper

        Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.3.1, Scenario 6.3.2 as you would in the exam. Then do the 5 numericals. Then try your own numbers in the labs.

        2Memorise sheet

        • Full-duplex, synchronous, very high speed, short-distance, on-board.
        • Single master only. Slide spec: 4 wires, 10 Mbps, 1 master, theoretically unlimited slaves.
        • MOSI master→slave, MISO slave→master, SCLK from master, SS/CS active low.
        • One bit per clock, so clock frequency = data rate.
        • Advantages: full duplex, fast, not limited to 8 bits, no start/stop bits, slave needs no oscillator, no conflict.
        • Disadvantages: 4 pins, single master, dedicated SS per slave, no acknowledgement, speed depends on device.
        • Uses: SD/MMC, EEPROM, Flash, sensors, ADC, audio codec, LCD, touchscreen.

        3Mnemonics & templates

        Four lines
        My Mom Seldom Sleeps = MOSI, MISO, SCLK, SS.
        Four steps of a transfer
        Cats Love Milk Mornings = Clock out, SS Low, MOSI bits, MISO bits.
        Template: 5-mark "how SPI works"
        1. Draw master and slave shift registers in a ring. 2. Master generates SCLK. 3. Master pulls the slave's SS low. 4. Each clock shifts one bit out on MOSI and one in on MISO. 5. Master raises SS to finish. State the mode (CPOL, CPHA).

        4Diagrams & symbol checklist

        Tick each symbol once you can draw it from memory.

        ModeCPOLCPHA
        000
        101
        210
        311

        5Keyword → function → diagram

        KeywordArduino function / conceptDiagram
        "initialise bus"SPI.begin()Master block
        "send and receive a byte"SPI.transfer(val)MOSI + MISO arrows
        "select the device"digitalWrite(SS, LOW)SS̄ line to slave
        "clock speed / divide"SPI.setClockDivider(SPI_CLOCK_DIV8)SCLK label

        6Numericals

        Numerical 1

        Arduino SPI clock

        16 MHz board with SPI_CLOCK_DIV8. Find SCLK and byte time.

        Solution

        SCLK = 16 MHz / 8 = 2 MHz. One byte = 8 clocks = 8/2 MHz = 4 µs.

        Numerical 2

        Transfer time

        Read 1 KB (1024 bytes) from Flash at 8 MHz, ignoring command overhead.

        Solution

        Bits = 1024 × 8 = 8192. Time = 8192 / 8 MHz = 1.024 ms.

        Numerical 3

        Master pin count

        Six slaves. Compare independent and daisy chain.

        Solution

        Independent = MOSI + MISO + SCLK + 6 SS = 9 pins. Daisy = MOSI + MISO + SCLK + 1 SS = 4 pins.

        Numerical 4

        Daisy-chain clocks

        Four 8-bit slaves in a chain, each to get one new byte.

        Solution

        Data must ripple through every slave, so 4 × 8 = 32 clocks with SS held low. At 1 MHz that is 32 µs.

        Numerical 5

        SPI vs I²C for a display

        Send 100 bytes. SPI at 4 MHz vs I²C at 400 kHz.

        Solution

        SPI: 800 bits / 4 MHz = 200 µs. I²C: address frame + 100 data frames = 101 × 9 = 909 clocks / 400 kHz ≈ 2.27 ms. SPI is about 11× faster here.

        7Solved scenarios

        Scenario 6.3.1Built like your FAT10 marks

        High-speed data logger

        A vibration logger streams samples from an ADC to an SD card and also drives a small LCD, all on one MCU. (a) Justify SPI over I²C and UART. 3 M (b) Draw the bus with all connections and name the configuration. 4 M (c) Explain how the MCU talks to only the ADC. 3 M

        Solution
        Decode the question: "streams" → high speed + full duplex → SPI. "ADC, SD card, LCD" → 3 slaves → independent configuration, 3 SS lines.

        (a) 3M Streaming needs speed. SPI is full duplex and has no start/stop or address overhead. I²C is slower with ack and address overhead. UART is point-to-point with one slave only.

        (b) 4M

        (c) 3M All SS lines are idle high. The MCU pulls only SS1 low, so only the ADC responds. The others keep MISO in high impedance. The MCU generates SCLK, and data shifts on MOSI and MISO. It raises SS1 when done. digitalWrite(SS1,LOW); x=SPI.transfer(0); digitalWrite(SS1,HIGH);

        Scenario 6.3.2Built like your FAT10 marks

        Too few GPIO pins for eight LED drivers

        A signboard controller must update eight 8-bit LED driver chips but has only one free select pin. (a) Choose the configuration and draw it. 4 M (b) Compute update time at 2 MHz. 2 M (c) Give two risks of SPI here, and the mitigation. 2 M (d) State SPI's clock parameters. 2 M

        Solution

        (a) 4M Daisy chain. Master MOSI → S1 MOSI, S1 MISO → S2 MOSI … S8 MISO → master MISO. SCLK and one SS̄ are common to all.

        (b) 2M 8 × 8 = 64 clocks. 64 / 2 MHz = 32 µs.

        (c) 2M No acknowledgement, so a failed chip goes unnoticed. Mitigate by reading back the chained data on MISO. One broken chip breaks the chain, so add a test or bypass point.

        (d) 2M CPOL is the clock idle level. CPHA selects the edge used to read data. Together they give modes 0–3, and master and slave must match.

        8Tips & traps

        Slide check: Your slide 31 has a wiring typo: It says master *MISO* goes to slave 1 *MOSI*. The real connection is master MOSI → slave 1 MOSI. Draw it this way.
        Slide check: Bit order: Slide 28 says master→slave is MSB first and slave→master is LSB first. Bit order is really a setting (MSBFIRST/LSBFIRST). If asked directly, quote the slide and add "configurable".
        Tip: "No ACK" and "needs SS per slave" are the two best one-liners against SPI.
        MODULE 6 · UNIT 4

        I²C

        Two wires, many devices, every device with its own address. A full FAT question.

        PYQ: Q5 (10 M)Scenario theoryTiming numericals
        How it comes in the exam

        Q5 was entirely I²C: arbitration + integrity 5M, master/slave roles 2M, SDA/SCL 3M, wrapped in a smart-home story. Learn the 6 steps and the arbitration argument.

        Your path through this unit

        Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

          1Learn it, step by step

          Lesson 1

          Two wires shared by everyone

          In plain words

          Imagine a classroom with one shared whiteboard (SDA) and a teacher tapping a ruler to set the pace (SCL). Everyone can see it, so each message starts with a name, and only that person responds. That name is the address.

          The lines are normally pulled high by resistors. Devices can only pull them low. This matters later for arbitration.

          Write this in the exam
          • I²C was invented in 1989 by Philips. Two wires: SDA (bidirectional data) and SCL (clock).
          • Synchronous. The master controls the clock signal. Supports multi-master and multi-slave.
          • Short distance, intra-board communication.

          Remember: SDA = data · SCL = clock · pull-ups keep both high.

          Check yourself: Why are pull-up resistors needed?

          Devices only pull lines low. The resistors return them high when no device is pulling.

          Lesson 2

          The message: start, address, data, stop

          In plain words

          A message is like a phone call. Start: dial. Address: "Is that the temperature sensor?" ACK: "Yes, speaking." Data: the conversation, with a "got it" after each sentence. Stop: hang up.

          Write this in the exam
          • Start: SDA goes high to low before SCL goes low. Stop: SDA goes low to high after SCL goes high.
          • Address frame: 7 or 10 bits, unique per slave.
          • R/W bit: 0 = master sends, 1 = master receives.
          • ACK/NACK after each frame.

          Remember: SARA DAP: Start, Address, R/W, ACK, Data, ACK, stoP.

          Check yourself: Slave 0x48: what byte does the master send to read from it?

          (0x48 << 1) + 1 = 0x91.

          Lesson 3

          The six steps of a transfer

          In plain words

          Each step below is one mark-worthy line. Learn them in order, and you can write "how I²C works" from memory.

          Write this in the exam
          1. Master sets the start condition.
          2. Master sends the 7 or 10-bit address with the R/W bit.
          3. Each slave compares it to its own address. The matching slave pulls SDA low (ACK). Others leave it high.
          4. Master sends or receives the data frame.
          5. After each frame, the receiving device sends an ACK.
          6. Master sets the stop condition: SCL high, then SDA high.

          Remember: Start → Address → ACK → Data → ACK → Stop.

          Check yourself: What does a slave do if the address doesn't match?

          It leaves SDA high and ignores the rest of the message.

          Lesson 4

          Arbitration: when two masters talk at once

          In plain words

          Remember that devices can only pull lines low, so if anyone pulls low, the line is low. That's called wired-AND. Each master listens while it talks. If a master tries to send a 1 but reads a 0, somebody else is sending a 0, so it knows it lost and goes quiet. The winner never even notices, and its message isn't damaged.

          Write this in the exam
          • Open-drain lines with pull-ups form a wired-AND bus: a 0 from any device overrides a 1.
          • Each master monitors SDA while sending. One that sends 1 but reads 0 loses arbitration and releases the bus.
          • The winning master's data is not corrupted.
          • Integrity: ACK/NACK per byte, SDA stable while SCL is high, unique Start/Stop.

          Remember: Low wins. If you wrote 1 and read 0, quit.

          Check yourself: Master A sends 1 and Master B sends 0 on the same bit. Who continues?

          B. A reads 0 instead of its 1 and backs off.

          Lesson 5

          Wire library, and I²C's trade-offs

          In plain words

          On Arduino Uno, SDA is A4 and SCL is A5. The master asks with requestFrom. The slave answers through a handler function that runs automatically when the master asks.

          Write this in the exam
          • Wire.begin() joins as master, Wire.begin(8) as slave #8.
          • Wire.requestFrom(8, 6) requests 6 bytes. Wire.read() reads. Wire.write() sends.
          • Wire.onRequest(handler), Wire.onReceive(handler) register slave handlers.
          • Advantages: 2 wires, multi-master/slave, addressing, ACK/NACK. Disadvantages: slower than SPI, pull-up power and clock limits, frame overhead.

          Remember: Master asks. Slave's handler answers.

          Check yourself: I²C or SPI for 5 slow sensors with 2 spare pins?

          I²C: two wires regardless of device count.

          Final step

          Practice on paper

          Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.4.1, Scenario 6.4.2, Scenario 6.4.3 as you would in the exam. Then do the 5 numericals. Then try your own numbers in the labs.

          2Memorise sheet

          • Philips, 1989. Two wires: SDA (bidirectional data), SCL (clock). Short distance, intra-board.
          • Synchronous, multi-master + multi-slave.
          • Message = Start, 7 or 10-bit address, R/W, ACK, data frames each with ACK, Stop.
          • Start: SDA falls while SCL high. Stop: SDA rises while SCL high.
          • R/W: 0 = master writes, 1 = master reads.
          • ACK: receiver pulls SDA low. Address mismatch: slave leaves SDA high (NACK).
          • Advantages: 2 wires, multi-master, addressing, ACK/NACK, works with slow and fast ICs.
          • Disadvantages: slower than SPI, pull-up power and speed limits, multi-master complexity, frame overhead.
          • Arduino Uno: SDA = A4, SCL = A5.

          3Mnemonics & templates

          Frame
          SARA DAP = Start, Address, R/W, ACK, Data, ACK, stoP.
          Arbitration
          "Low wins. If you wrote 1 and read 0, quit."
          Template: Six steps (5 marks, 1 line each + diagram)
          1. Master makes Start. 2. Master sends address + R/W. 3. Matching slave pulls SDA low (ACK). 4. Data frame sent or received. 5. Receiver ACKs each byte. 6. Master makes Stop.

          4Diagrams & symbol checklist

          Tick each symbol once you can draw it from memory.

          5Keyword → function → diagram

          KeywordWire function / conceptDiagram
          "join the bus"Wire.begin() / Wire.begin(8)Node on bus
          "master requests bytes"Wire.requestFrom(8, 6)Arrow S→M
          "read received byte"Wire.read()Box after request
          "master sends to slave"Wire.beginTransmission(a), Wire.write(), Wire.endTransmission()Arrow M→S
          "when master asks, slave replies"Wire.onRequest(handler)ISR-style box
          "slave gets data"Wire.onReceive(handler)Handler box
          "minimal wiring, many sensors"I²C bus2 lines + pull-ups
          "two masters at once"ArbitrationWired-AND note
          "speed setting"Wire.setClock()SCL label

          6Numericals

          Numerical 1

          Address byte on the wire

          Slave 0x48. Find the byte sent for write and for read.

          Solution

          Shift left by one and add R/W. 0x48 << 1 = 0x90. Write = 0x90, Read = 0x91.

          Numerical 2

          How many devices?

          Compare 7-bit and 10-bit addressing.

          Solution

          2^7 = 128 addresses (112 usable, since 16 are reserved). 2^10 = 1024.

          Numerical 3

          Write time

          Write 2 data bytes at 100 kHz.

          Solution

          Frames = address + 2 data = 3 × 9 = 27 clocks, + about 2 for Start/Stop = 29. Time = 29 × 10 µs = 290 µs.

          Numerical 4

          Read 6 bytes (the Wire example) at 400 kHz

          Solution

          7 frames × 9 = 63 + 2 = 65 clocks. 65 × 2.5 µs = 162.5 µs.

          Numerical 5

          Pull-up range

          Vcc 5 V, VOL 0.4 V, IOL 3 mA, bus 200 pF, rise time 1 µs.

          Solution

          Rmin = (5 − 0.4)/3 mA = 1.53 kΩ. Rmax = tr/(0.8473·Cb) = 1000 ns/(0.8473 × 200 pF) = 5.9 kΩ. Choose 4.7 kΩ. (The formula is standard, beyond your slides.)

          7Solved PYQ scenarios

          Scenario 6.4.1PYQ Q510 marks

          Smart home sensors and actuators on one bus

          Sensors (temperature, humidity, light) and actuators (LEDs, motors) talk to a central MCU over I²C, with minimal wiring and proper addressing. (a) Analyse how I²C transmits data on the shared bus, including arbitration and data integrity. 5 M (b) MCU is master, the rest slaves: evaluate roles in addressing and how each device knows when to send or receive. 2 M (c) Explain the purpose of SDA and SCL and how they synchronise transfer. 3 M

          Solution
          Decode the question: "Shared bus" → draw 2 lines + pull-ups. "arbitration" → wired-AND. "integrity" → ACK + stable SDA. "knows when" → address match + R/W bit.

          (a) 5M

          Data moves as messages. Master issues Start, sends a 7-bit address + R/W, the addressed slave returns ACK, then 8-bit data frames each followed by ACK, then Stop.

          Arbitration: lines are open-drain with pull-ups, forming a wired-AND, so a 0 from any device beats a 1. Each master reads SDA as it transmits. A master that sends 1 but reads 0 has lost and releases the bus immediately. The winner's message isn't corrupted.

          Integrity: (i) ACK/NACK after every byte, so failures are detected and retried; (ii) SDA changes only while SCL is low and is stable while SCL is high; (iii) Start and Stop are unique patterns, so frames are clearly bounded.

          (b) 2M The master starts every transfer, generates the clock and chooses the slave. Each slave has a unique address and compares it after Start. Only the match responds. The R/W bit then tells it to receive (0) or send (1).

          (c) 3M SDA carries address, data and ACK bits both ways, e.g. the temperature byte up and motor commands down. SCL is the master's clock, and each pulse moves one bit. Receivers sample while SCL is high, so transmitter and receiver stay in step without a shared baud rate. Slow sensors may hold SCL low (clock stretching) until ready.

          Scenario 6.4.2Built like your FAT10 marks

          Sensor hub: choose the frame and write the master

          A weather station MCU reads 6 bytes from a slave at address 8 every 500 ms. (a) Draw the message frame. 3 M (b) Write Arduino master and slave code. 5 M (c) A sensor's address was wrongly set. What happens on the bus? 2 M

          Solution

          (a) 3M S, 0001000 (addr), R/W = 1, A, then 6 data bytes each followed by master A (last by Ā), P.

          (b) 5M

          // MASTER
#include <Wire.h>
void setup(){ Wire.begin(); Serial.begin(9600); }
void loop(){
  Wire.requestFrom(8, 6);
  while (Wire.available()) { char c = Wire.read(); Serial.print(c); }
  delay(500);
}
// SLAVE
#include <Wire.h>
void setup(){ Wire.begin(8); Wire.onRequest(requestEvent); }
void loop(){ delay(100); }
void requestEvent(){ Wire.write("hello "); }   // 6 bytes

          (c) 2M No slave matches, so SDA stays high at the ACK slot. The master sees NACK, issues Stop and can retry or flag a fault.

          Scenario 6.4.3Built like your FAT10 marks

          Choosing I²C or SPI for a wearable

          A wearable reads a heart-rate sensor and an accelerometer 50 times a second and has 2 free pins. (a) Choose the bus. 3 M (b) Show bus utilisation at 100 kHz, 6 bytes per sensor per read. 4 M (c) Give two drawbacks and the design response. 3 M

          Solution

          (a) 3M I²C. It needs only 2 wires however many sensors there are. SPI needs 3 + N pins, which won't fit. Low data rate suits I²C.

          (b) 4M One read = 7 frames × 9 + 2 = 65 clocks. Two sensors = 130 clocks per cycle. ×50 = 6500 clocks/s. Utilisation = 6500/100000 = 6.5 %, so there's ample margin.

          (c) 3M Pull-ups waste power, so use the largest valid value. Limited clock speed, so keep the 400 kHz mode in reserve.

          8Tips & traps

          Slide check: Slide 48: "Master addresses slaves via SCL" is loose wording. The address actually travels on SDA, and SCL only clocks it. Write SDA.
          Trap: Start/Stop are the only times SDA changes while SCL is high. State this rule and you've covered "synchronisation" and "integrity" together.
          Tip: Q5's marks were 5+2+3. Don't over-write the 2-marker. Put your effort into arbitration.
          MODULE 6 · UNIT 5

          CAN

          The bus inside every car: no master, and the most urgent message always wins.

          FrameArbitration + stuffing numericalsLinks to ABS and airbag
          How it comes in the exam

          No CAN question on your paper, but the deck is 30 slides long, and the frame, arbitration and stuffing are very askable. It connects directly to Module 7 (ABS, airbag).

          Your path through this unit

          Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

            1Learn it, step by step

            Lesson 1

            Why cars needed CAN

            In plain words

            A car has dozens of computers (ECUs). Wiring each to each other would need kilometres of cable. CAN is one shared two-wire "party line". Each message is labelled by *what it is*, not *who it's for*, and every ECU listens and keeps only what it needs.

            Write this in the exam
            • CAN lets all ECUs communicate via a single two-wire bus: CAN High and CAN Low.
            • Need: simple and low cost, centralised, robust to EMI, efficient prioritisation through IDs.
            • Multi-master: master-slave is not used. A unique ID replaces the destination address.
            • Good speed: 1 Mbit/s at 40 m. Nodes can be added without re-programming.

            Remember: CAN labels the message, not the receiver.

            Check yourself: How does a CAN node know a message is for it?

            All nodes receive every frame and each decides from the ID whether to accept it.

            Lesson 2

            Inside a CAN node

            In plain words

            Each node has three layers. The host is the brain. The CAN controller turns data into correctly formatted frames. The transceiver turns those bits into signals on the actual wires.

            Write this in the exam
            • CAN uses the lower two OSI layers: physical and data link.
            • Host controller: application layer. CAN controller: LLC and MAC.
            • LLC filters messages by unique ID. MAC does framing, arbitration, error detection, acknowledgement.
            • Transceiver handles encoding and decoding and synchronises with the bus.

            Remember: Host → Controller → Transceiver → Bus.

            Check yourself: Which sub-layer filters messages by ID?

            LLC.

            Lesson 3

            The frame, field by field

            In plain words

            A frame is a fixed form with boxes in a fixed order. Dominant means logic 0, and recessive means logic 1. Those names matter because a dominant bit physically overrides a recessive one.

            Write this in the exam
            • SOF: one dominant bit marking the start and synchronising nodes. Identifier: priority and message type.
            • RTR: dominant for data frame, recessive for remote frame. IDE: dominant for standard.
            • DLC: 4-bit data length. CRC: checksum. ACK: receiver overwrites the recessive slot with dominant.
            • EOF: 7 bits. IFS: 3 recessive bits.
            • Standard = 11-bit ID. Extended = 29-bit ID, adding SRR and R1.
            • Four frame types: Data, Remote, Error, Overload.

            Remember: Bit count: 47 + 8n before stuffing.

            Check yourself: How many bits is a 2-byte standard frame before stuffing?

            47 + 16 = 63.

            Lesson 4

            Arbitration: lowest ID wins

            In plain words

            Two ECUs start at once. Each sends its ID bit by bit while listening. A dominant 0 beats a recessive 1, so whoever sends a 1 and hears a 0 stops and waits. The message with the most leading zeros, the lowest ID, simply carries on. Nothing is destroyed, and no time is wasted.

            Write this in the exam
            • Non-destructive bitwise arbitration, handled by the identifier and RTR bits.
            • Highest priority message gets the bus. Lower priority nodes wait till the bus is free.
            • ID bits are sent from ID10 down to ID0.

            Remember: Lower ID = higher priority.

            Check yourself: IDs 0x100 and 0x0FF collide. Who wins?

            0x0FF, which has the lower value.

            Lesson 5

            Bit stuffing and fault confinement

            In plain words

            Long runs of the same bit make receivers lose their timing. So after five identical bits, the sender adds one opposite bit, and the receiver removes it again.

            A faulty node shouldn't jam a whole car, so each node counts its own errors. Too many and it steps back, and eventually disconnects itself.

            Write this in the exam
            • Bit stuffing: after 5 bits of identical value, insert a bit of opposite value.
            • Errors: bit error, stuff error, CRC/ACK/EOF/error/overload delimiter errors.
            • States: Error Active (REC and TEC under 128), Error Passive (over 127), Bus Off (TEC over 255).

            Remember: Five the same → stuff one opposite.

            Check yourself: Stuff the bits 111111.

            11111 0 1: after five 1s insert a 0, then the last 1.

            Final step

            Practice on paper

            Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.5.1, Scenario 6.5.2, Scenario 6.5.3 as you would in the exam. Then do the 5 numericals. Then try your own numbers in the labs.

            2Memorise sheet

            • Two wires, CAN High + CAN Low. All ECUs on one bus. Multi-master, no master-slave.
            • Dominant = 0, Recessive = 1. Dominant wins.
            • Messages carry an ID, not a destination. All nodes receive and filter by ID. Nodes can be added without reprogramming.
            • Uses OSI layers 1–2. CAN controller = LLC + MAC. Transceiver = encode/decode on the bus. Host = application.
            • 1 Mbit/s at 40 m. Standard = 11-bit ID, Extended = 29-bit ID.
            • Advantages: low cost, EMI immune, flexible, multi-master, fault confinement, broadcast.
            • Four frames: Data, Remote, Error, Overload.
            • Stuffing: after 5 identical bits insert one opposite bit.

            3Mnemonics & templates

            Standard frame
            Some Idiots Run In Rain Daily, Drenching Cars And Every Inch = SOF, ID, RTR, IDE, r0, DLC, Data, CRC, ACK, EOF, IFS.
            Frame types
            DREO = Data, Remote, Error, Overload.
            Template: Field bit lengths: say them in order

            1, 11, 1, 1, 1, 4, 0–64, 16, 2, 7, 3 → total 47 + 8n bits before stuffing. 8 bytes = 111 bits.

            4Diagrams & symbol checklist

            Tick each symbol once you can draw it from memory.

            5Keyword → function → diagram

            KeywordMaps toDiagram
            "priority, urgent message"Lower ID winsArbitration bit table
            "no master"Multi-master, broadcastCommon bus
            "request data from a node"Remote frame, RTR recessiveFrame with no data field
            "node too busy"Overload frameDelay between frames
            "faulty node"TEC/REC, bus offState diagram
            "more IDs needed"Extended 29-bit, SRR, IDELonger arbitration field
            "noisy environment"Differential pair, CRC, stuffingCANH/CANL + 120 Ω
            "same polarity for 5 bits"Stuff bitStuffed waveform

            6Numericals

            Numerical 1

            Arbitration

            Node A ID 0x65A, B ID 0x658, C ID 0x6FF. Who wins?

            Solution

            Binary: A 110 0101 1010, B 110 0101 1000, C 110 1111 1111. Bits agree until C sends 1 at ID7 while A, B send 0, so C drops out. A and B differ at ID1: A sends 1, B sends 0, so A drops. B wins, having the lowest ID.

            Numerical 2

            Frame length and time

            8-byte standard frame at 500 kbit/s, no stuffing.

            Solution

            47 + 8×8 = 111 bits. Time = 111/500k = 222 µs.

            Numerical 3

            Bit stuffing

            Stuff 0000011111000001.

            Solution

            Result: 00000 1 1111 0 1 00000 1 1. Stuffed: 0000011111010000011 (3 stuff bits, 19 bits). The inserted bit itself counts toward the next run, which is why the second stuff comes after only four original 1s.

            Numerical 4

            Worst-case stuffing

            8-byte frame, stuffing applies SOF through CRC sequence.

            Solution

            Stuffed region = 34 + 64 = 98 bits. Worst stuff bits = ⌊(98 − 1)/4⌋ = 24. Worst frame = 111 + 24 = 135 bits.

            Numerical 5

            Max message rate

            At 1 Mbit/s, using 111-bit frames, how many frames per second?

            Solution

            1 000 000/111 ≈ 9009 frames/s with no stuffing or gaps beyond IFS. Include real overhead in a design.

            7Solved scenarios

            Scenario 6.5.1Built like your FAT10 marks

            Car: airbag vs. window message

            An airbag ECU (ID 0x010) and a window ECU (ID 0x300) start transmitting at the same moment on a CAN bus. (a) Show how CAN resolves this, with bit-level reasoning. 4 M (b) Draw the frame and explain each field. 4 M (c) Why doesn't the window message get lost? 2 M

            Solution
            Decode the question: "same moment" → arbitration. "IDs" → write binaries. Lower number = higher priority = airbag.

            (a) 4M

            Bit10987…0
            Airbag 0x01000000010000
            Window 0x30001100000000
            Bus000…

            At ID9 the window node sends recessive 1 and reads dominant 0, so it stops transmitting. The airbag continues unharmed. This is non-destructive bitwise arbitration.

            (b) 4M Draw the 11-field strip. SOF syncs. ID = priority + type. RTR = data/remote. IDE = format. DLC = bytes. Data ≤ 8 bytes. CRC = error detection. ACK slot overwritten by receivers. EOF ends. IFS = 3-bit gap.

            (c) 2M The losing node just becomes a receiver and retries automatically when the bus is free. No data was destroyed.

            Scenario 6.5.2Built like your FAT10 marks

            A CAN node keeps failing

            A wheel-speed ECU has a damaged transceiver and keeps sending corrupted frames. (a) List error types CAN detects. 3 M (b) Explain the error frame. 3 M (c) Draw the fault confinement states. 4 M

            Solution

            (a) 3M Physical: bit error, stuff error. Frame: CRC delimiter, ACK delimiter, end of frame, error delimiter, overload delimiter errors.

            (b) 3M A node that detects an error aborts and sends an error frame: an error flag (superimposed, 0–12 dominant bits) followed by an 8-bit recessive delimiter. All nodes discard the frame and the sender retries.

            (c) 4M

            Passive returns to Active when both counters fall under 128. Bus OFF returns to Active after a normal-mode request and 128 occurrences of 11 recessive bits. So the bad ECU isolates itself and stops disturbing the bus.

            Scenario 6.5.3Built like your FAT10 marks

            Why CAN over point-to-point wiring

            A carmaker is moving 10 ECUs from point-to-point wiring to CAN. (a) Compare wiring and justify. 3 M (b) Draw the node's internal architecture. 4 M (c) How can a new ECU be added late in the design? 3 M

            Solution

            (a) 3M Point-to-point for 10 fully linked ECUs needs 10×9/2 = 45 links. CAN uses a single two-wire bus with one point of entry. It is cheaper, lighter, EMI robust and prioritised.

            (b) 4M

            LLC filters messages by ID. MAC handles framing, arbitration, error detection and ACK.

            (c) 3M Nodes filter by ID and frames don't name a destination, so a new node simply listens to the IDs it needs. Existing nodes need no reprogramming.

            8Tips & traps

            Trap: Lower ID = higher priority. Dominant (0) means a 0 early in the ID wins.
            Tip: Always write "non-destructive". It's the phrase examiners look for in CAN arbitration.
            Trap: The slide lists CRC as 16 bits: that's 15 CRC + 1 delimiter. DATA is up to 64 bits = 8 bytes.
            MODULE 6 · UNIT 6

            Ethernet

            The wired network standard. This deck comes with worked address and frame examples.

            NumericalsTables to memoriseHub → switch design
            How it comes in the exam

            The deck has worked examples and summary tables, making it the most numerical part of Module 6. Expect address classification, frame length/padding, and a hub→switch design story.

            Your path through this unit

            Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

              1Learn it, step by step

              Lesson 1

              IEEE 802 and four generations

              In plain words

              Different companies needed their equipment to work together, so IEEE wrote Project 802. It only deals with the bottom two layers. The data link layer is split in two: the LLC top half is shared, and MAC differs for each kind of network.

              Write this in the exam
              • Project 802 (1985) specifies the physical and data link layer functions of major LAN protocols.
              • Ethernet started in 1976 at Xerox PARC.
              • Four generations: Standard 10 Mbps, Fast 100 Mbps, Gigabit 1 Gbps, Ten-Gigabit 10 Gbps.

              Remember: Data link = LLC + MAC.

              Check yourself: What standard name is Fast Ethernet? Gigabit?

              Fast is 802.3u. Gigabit is 802.3z.

              Lesson 2

              The 802.3 frame and its length limits

              In plain words

              A frame is an envelope: wake-up pattern, addresses, length, letter, and a checksum. If your letter is very short, Ethernet adds padding so the frame stays long enough for collisions to be noticed.

              Write this in the exam
              • Preamble 7 bytes (56 alternating bits), SFD 1 byte (10101011), DA 6, SA 6, Length/Type 2, Data 46–1500, CRC 4.
              • Frame length: minimum 64 bytes (512 bits), maximum 1518 bytes (12144 bits).

              Remember: 7-1-6-6-2-data-4.

              Check yourself: 30 bytes of data: how much padding?

              46 − 30 = 16 bytes.

              Lesson 3

              Addresses: unicast, multicast, broadcast

              In plain words

              An Ethernet address is 48 bits, usually written in hex pairs. The very last bit of the first byte is a flag: 0 for one receiver, 1 for a group. Conveniently, that's visible from the second hex digit alone: even means unicast, odd means multicast.

              Write this in the exam
              • Address = 6 bytes = 12 hex digits = 48 bits.
              • LSB of the first byte: 0 unicast, otherwise multicast.
              • Broadcast is a special case of multicast in which all bits are 1s.
              • Sent left to right byte by byte. Within each byte, right to left bit by bit.

              Remember: Second digit even = unicast.

              Check yourself: Classify 3B:00:11:22:33:44.

              B = 1011, odd, so multicast.

              Lesson 4

              From shared cable to switches

              In plain words

              On a shared cable only one station can talk, and everyone splits the bandwidth. A bridge cuts the cable into smaller groups. A switch gives each station a private link. With separate send and receive paths (full duplex), collisions disappear altogether.

              Write this in the exam
              • Bridges divide a network into smaller collision domains and raise bandwidth per station.
              • Switched Ethernet: each station is its own collision domain.
              • Full-duplex: transmit and receive are separate. There's no collision, so cable length is set by attenuation.

              Remember: Hub shares · Bridge splits · Switch dedicates.

              Check yourself: 8 stations on a 10 Mbps switch. Bandwidth each?

              10 Mbps each, dedicated.

              Lesson 5

              Reading implementation names and encoding

              In plain words

              Names follow a pattern. 10Base5 means 10 Mbps, baseband, 500 m. Faster links use block codes that add a few extra bits so the receiver always sees enough transitions to keep its timing. The tables are in the memorise sheet below.

              Write this in the exam
              • Standard Ethernet uses Manchester encoding.
              • 100Base-TX: 4B/5B + MLT-3. 100Base-FX: 4B/5B + NRZ-I. 100Base-T4: 8B/6T.
              • 1000Base-SX/LX/CX: 8B/10B + NRZ. 1000Base-T: 4D-PAM5.

              Remember: More speed → block coding to retain transitions.

              Check yourself: What's the maximum length of 10Base-T?

              100 m.

              Final step

              Practice on paper

              Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.6.1, Scenario 6.6.2 as you would in the exam. Then do the 5 numericals. Then try your own numbers in the labs.

              6Numericals

              Numerical 1

              Classify destination addresses (your deck's type)

              a) 4A:30:10:21:10:1A b) 47:20:1B:2E:08:EE c) FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF

              Solution

              Check the second hex digit. a) A = 1010, even: unicast. b) 7 = 0111, odd: multicast. c) all Fs: broadcast.

              Numerical 2

              Bit order on the line

              Show 47:20:1B:2E:08:EE as sent.

              Solution

              Reverse the bits inside each byte, keep the byte order. 11100010 00000100 11011000 01110100 00010000 01110111

              Numerical 3

              Padding

              A sensor sends 20 bytes of data. Find padding, frame size and efficiency.

              Solution

              Padding = 46 − 20 = 26 bytes. Frame = 6+6+2+46+4 = 64 bytes. Efficiency = 20/64 = 31.25 %.

              Numerical 4

              Frame time at 10 Mbps

              Find transmission time for minimum and maximum frames.

              Solution

              Min 512 bits/10 Mbps = 51.2 µs. Max 12144 bits/10 Mbps = 1214.4 µs. Payload efficiency at max = 1500/1518 = 98.8 %. At min with 46 bytes = 46/64 = 71.9 %.

              Numerical 5

              Bridge bandwidth

              12 stations share 10 Mbps. A bridge splits them into 4 segments of 3.

              Solution

              Before: 10/12 = 0.83 Mbps each, 1 domain. After: 10/3 = 3.33 Mbps each, 4 domains (ignoring bridge load). With a switch: full 10 Mbps each.

              7Solved scenarios

              Scenario 6.6.1Built like your FAT10 marks

              Slow factory network on a shared coax

              A factory has 12 PLC stations on one 10 Mbps shared bus, with long delays during peak hours. (a) Explain why, with a diagram. 3 M (b) Propose bridged and then switched upgrades, and quantify per-station bandwidth. 4 M (c) How does full duplex change the medium access? 3 M

              Solution
              Decode the question: "shared / delays" → one collision domain. "upgrade" → bridge → switch → full duplex. Numbers: 10/12, 10/3, 10.

              (a) 3M All 12 stations are in one collision domain and share 10 Mbps, about 0.83 Mbps each. Peak traffic raises collisions and retries, so delay climbs.

              (b) 4M Bridged: 4 segments of 3 stations gives 4 domains and 10/3 = 3.33 Mbps each. Bridge filters local traffic. Switched (10Base-T star): each station is its own domain, dedicated 10 Mbps per link.

              (c) 3M With full-duplex links there are separate transmit and receive paths and no collisions, so CSMA/CD isn't needed. Each link can carry 10 Mbps each way. Cable length then depends on signal attenuation only.

              Scenario 6.6.2Built like your FAT10 marks

              Campus cabling choices

              A plant links machines 90 m from a switch, two buildings 400 m apart, and a data centre 8 km away. (a) Pick a standard for each, with reasons. 6 M (b) Explain 4B/5B or 8B/10B and why block coding is used. 4 M

              Solution

              (a) 6M

              LinkChooseWhy
              Machines, 90 m1000Base-T or 100Base-TXCopper within 100 m limit, cheap
              Buildings, 400 m1000Base-SXShort-wave fiber to 550 m; beyond copper
              Data centre, 8 km10GBase-LSingle-mode, to 10 km (1000Base-LX stops at 5 km)

              (b) 4M Block coding maps groups of bits to longer codes: 4→5 at 100 Mbps gives 125 Mbaud, 8→10 at 1 Gbps gives 1.25 Gbaud. The extra codes guarantee enough transitions for clock recovery and allow error detection, without the 2× baud cost of Manchester.

              8Tips & traps

              Trap: 1518 excludes the 8-byte preamble + SFD. On the wire the maximum is 1526 bytes.
              Tip: To classify an address, you only need the second hex digit. Don't convert the whole thing.
              MODULE 6 · UNIT 7

              ZigBee

              Tiny radios on batteries that can last for years, passing messages along a mesh.

              Design scenariosNumbers to memorise
              How it comes in the exam

              Typically a design question: "battery sensors over a farm or building, choose and justify". Know the three roles, topologies and numbers cold.

              Your path through this unit

              Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

                1Learn it, step by step

                Lesson 1

                What ZigBee is for

                In plain words

                Wi-Fi is like a highway: fast, and it drinks fuel. ZigBee is a bicycle: slow, but it runs for years on a tiny battery. It's perfect for a sensor that only needs to say "22 °C" once in a while.

                Write this in the exam
                • Built for control and sensor applications: very low cost, low power, low data rate, short range.
                • Works on IEEE 802.15.4. Bands: 868 MHz, 902–928 MHz, 2.4 GHz (16 channels).
                • 250 kbps. 10–100 m range. Up to 65,000 nodes in theory. AES-128 encryption.

                Remember: 2.4 GHz, 250 kbps, 65K nodes, AES-128.

                Check yourself: Why not Wi-Fi for a coin-cell door sensor?

                Wi-Fi has high power consumption and would drain the cell quickly.

                Lesson 2

                Three roles, three shapes of network

                In plain words

                Think of a company. The coordinator is the founder: exactly one, sets up the network. Routers are managers who pass messages along. End devices are staff who mostly sleep and only speak to their manager.

                Write this in the exam
                • Coordinator: root of the network, one per network, channel selection, assigns node IDs and addresses.
                • Router: intermediate node, routes traffic, allows others to join.
                • End device: sleep mode for battery efficiency. All its traffic goes via the parent.
                • Topologies: star, tree, mesh.

                Remember: Mains-powered = router · battery = end device.

                Check yourself: What happens to a mesh if one router dies?

                Traffic is routed through other routers.

                Lesson 3

                Sharing the channel, and the frame structure

                In plain words

                CSMA is polite conversation: listen first, and if someone's talking, wait a random time. GTS is a booked appointment: a guaranteed slot when you need certainty.

                Write this in the exam
                • Channel access: contention based (CSMA), or contention free (GTS).
                • Modes: beacon and beaconless. Beacons synchronise devices and carry superframe and GTS information.
                • MAC frame types: data, beacon, acknowledgement, command.

                Remember: CSMA = listen first · GTS = booked slot.

                Check yourself: Which is better for random button presses, beacon or beaconless?

                Beaconless with CSMA, since traffic is sporadic.

                Final step

                Practice on paper

                Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.7.1, Scenario 6.7.2 as you would in the exam. Then do the 5 numericals.

                2Memorise sheet

                • IEEE 802.15.4. Low cost, low power, low data rate, short range. For control and sensors.
                • Bands: 868 MHz (EU), 902–928 MHz (US, Australia), 2.4 GHz (worldwide). 16 channels at 2.4 GHz.
                • 250 kbps. Range 10–100 m (75–100 m indoor, up to 300 m outdoor line of sight).
                • Network: up to 65,000 nodes in theory. Join time 30 s per slide. AES-128.
                • Coordinator: root, one per network, picks channel, assigns IDs and addresses.
                • Router: intermediate, routes traffic, lets end devices join.
                • End device: sleeps to save battery. Traffic goes via its parent.
                • Topologies: star, tree, mesh. Modes: beacon, beaconless.
                • Channel access: contention based (CSMA) or contention free (GTS, guaranteed time slots).

                3Mnemonics & templates

                Roles
                CREam = Coordinator, Router, End device.
                Numbers
                "2.4, 250, 65K, AES-128", say it like a phone number.
                Template: Design answer

                Requirement → why ZigBee over Wi-Fi/Bluetooth → topology diagram with C/R/E → power strategy → channel access → security.

                4Diagrams & symbol checklist

                Tick each symbol once you can draw it from memory.

                5Keyword → function → diagram

                KeywordMaps toDiagram
                "battery for years"End device sleepE nodes at the edge
                "large area, nodes far apart"Mesh + routersMulti-hop lines
                "guaranteed latency"GTS, beacon modeSuperframe note
                "serial module on Arduino"SoftwareSerial XBee(2,3), XBee.write(), XBee.read()MCU→XBee via UART
                "sets up the network"CoordinatorRoot node

                6Numericals

                Numerical 1

                Packet time

                Largest PSDU at 250 kbps.

                Solution

                PSDU 1016 bits; with 48-bit PHY overhead = 1064 bits. Time = 1064/250k = 4.26 ms. Payload only = 4.06 ms.

                Numerical 2

                Daily airtime

                A node sends a 50-byte packet every 10 minutes at 250 kbps. Find on-air time per day.

                Solution

                50×8 = 400 bits + 48 = 448 bits → 1.79 ms. 144 packets/day × 1.79 ms = 258 ms/day, so the radio is almost always off.

                Numerical 3

                Bandwidth comparison (slide data)

                Time to send 1 KB by ZigBee 250 kbps, Bluetooth 1 Mbps, Wi-Fi 11 Mbps.

                Solution

                8192 bits. ZigBee 32.8 ms, Bluetooth 8.2 ms, Wi-Fi 0.74 ms. ZigBee is slowest but lowest in power.

                Numerical 4

                Address space

                How many nodes can a 16-bit short network address identify?

                Solution

                2^16 = 65,536, which is where the "up to 65,000 nodes" theoretical figure comes from.

                Numerical 5

                Battery life

                End device: 3 µA asleep, 30 mA for 2 ms once a minute, 1000 mAh cell.

                Solution

                Average = 3 µA + 30 mA × (2 ms / 60000 ms) = 3 + 1 = 4 µA. Life = 1000 mAh / 4 µA = 250,000 h ≈ 28.5 years. In reality the battery's shelf life limits it first, so say that.

                7Solved scenarios

                Scenario 6.7.1Built like your FAT10 marks

                Soil-moisture network on a 2 km farm

                A farm deploys 200 battery soil sensors over a large field, reporting every 15 minutes. (a) Justify ZigBee over Wi-Fi and Bluetooth. 3 M (b) Design the network with roles and topology diagram. 4 M (c) How do sensors last years on battery, and how is the channel accessed? 3 M

                Solution
                Decode the question: "200" → beyond Bluetooth's 7 active. "battery" → no Wi-Fi. "large" → mesh with routers.

                (a) 3M Low data, every 15 minutes, 250 kbps is ample. Wi-Fi has high power consumption. Bluetooth piconet has only 7 active slaves. ZigBee scales to 65,000 and is ultra low power.

                (b) 4M

                One coordinator at the farm office selects the channel and assigns addresses. Solar-powered routers on poles form a mesh, so a failed router gets routed around. Sensors are end devices joined to the nearest router.

                (c) 3M End devices sleep nearly all the time, waking for milliseconds to send. Parents hold traffic for them. Access is by CSMA: listen, send if clear, otherwise wait a random time. GTS can be used for slots that need a guarantee.

                Scenario 6.7.2Built like your FAT10 marks

                Smart lighting across a floor

                A floor has 60 lights, switches and occupancy sensors. (a) Assign ZigBee roles to the devices. 3 M (b) Draw the MAC data frame and explain 3 fields. 3 M (c) Choose beacon or beaconless, and state the security approach. 4 M

                Solution

                (a) 3M Controller hub = coordinator. Mains-powered lights = routers, giving a free mesh. Battery switches and occupancy sensors = end devices.

                (b) 3M Frame control (2), sequence number (1), address info (4–20), payload, FCS (2). Frame control identifies frame type. Sequence number matches ACKs. FCS detects errors.

                (c) 4M Beaconless with CSMA suits sporadic traffic such as a switch press, with no periodic overhead. Beacon mode with GTS would only be needed for time-critical traffic. Security: AES-128 at the network layer.

                8Tips & traps

                Slide check: Slides give the data rate as both "250 kbps" and "200–250 kbps", and range as 10–100 m and 75–100 m. Write 250 kbps and 10–100 m.
                Tip: Mains-powered = router, battery = end device. That one sentence gets you the design marks.
                MODULE 6 · UNIT 8

                Bluetooth

                One phone, up to seven gadgets: how they find each other and how they talk.

                StackACL vs SCOHC-05 code
                How it comes in the exam

                Common asks: draw the stack, explain ACL vs SCO, connection process, modes, or use HC-05 with Arduino.

                Your path through this unit

                Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

                  1Learn it, step by step

                  Lesson 1

                  Piconets: one master, seven slaves

                  In plain words

                  A piconet is a small group with one leader. Slaves can't chat among themselves, and everything goes through the master. Devices find each other without any fixed infrastructure.

                  Write this in the exam
                  • Bluetooth is a 2.4 GHz wireless link: short range, low power, low cost.
                  • One master can connect to up to seven slaves. Slaves transmit only to their master.
                  • Each device has a unique 48-bit address, BD_ADDR.
                  • Networks are called piconets and scatternets.

                  Remember: 1 master + 7 active slaves.

                  Check yourself: Why can only 7 slaves be active?

                  The 3-bit AM_ADDR gives 8 values, and 0 is reserved for broadcast.

                  Lesson 2

                  The protocol stack

                  In plain words

                  Each layer does one job for the layer above. The Radio makes the waves, and Baseband handles packets and timing. LMP sets up links, L2CAP splits and reassembles data, and RFCOMM pretends to be a serial cable.

                  Write this in the exam
                  • Radio: 2.4 GHz transceiver, frequency hopping, modulation. Baseband: addressing, packet format, timing, power.
                  • LMP: link set-up, authentication, encryption. HCI: command interface to baseband and link manager.
                  • L2CAP: multiplexing, segmentation and reassembly, QoS. RFCOMM: emulates serial ports. SDP: service discovery. TCS: telephony.

                  Remember: Real Bands Love Hearing Live Rock Shows Tonight Always.

                  Check yourself: Which layer finds out what services a device offers?

                  SDP.

                  Lesson 3

                  ACL, SCO and the packet

                  In plain words

                  Two kinds of traffic need different care. A file must arrive perfectly, even if late. A voice call must arrive on time, even if a little is lost. ACL is the file link. SCO is the voice link.

                  Write this in the exam
                  • ACL: packet-switched, one link per slave, correct delivery preferred, max 721 kbps.
                  • SCO: real-time, damaged packets aren't retransmitted, 64 kbps.
                  • Header: AM_ADDR 3, Type 4, Flow 1, ARQN 1, SEQN 1, HEC 8 = 18 bits, repeated 3× = 54 bits.

                  Remember: Files = ACL · voice = SCO.

                  Check yourself: A wireless earbud's music vs a call: which uses SCO?

                  The call: real-time voice.

                  Lesson 4

                  Connecting, power modes and HC-05

                  In plain words

                  First find them (Inquiry), then call them (Paging), then talk (Connection). After that, a device can doze in stages to save battery.

                  Write this in the exam
                  • Modes: Active; Sniff (recurring fixed slots); Hold (one-off sleep); Park (sleep until master wakes, up to 255 devices).
                  • Classes: 1 = 100 mW, 100 m; 2 = 2.5 mW, 10 m; 3 = 1 mW, 10 cm.
                  • HC-05: SPP module over UART. Default slave, 9600 8N1, PIN 1234. Role is set by AT commands.

                  Remember: A Snail Has Patience: Active, Sniff, Hold, Park.

                  Check yourself: Which mode frees a slave for one predetermined time?

                  Hold.

                  Final step

                  Practice on paper

                  Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.8.1, Scenario 6.8.2 as you would in the exam. Then do the 4 numericals. Then try your own numbers in the labs.
