                  6Numericals

                  Numerical 1

                  dBm to mW

                  Find power for 20, 4 and 0 dBm.

                  Solution

                  P = 10^(dBm/10) mW. 20 → 100 mW. 4 → 2.51 mW. 0 → 1 mW.

                  Numerical 2

                  Max packet

                  Largest packet, and time at 1 Mbps.

                  Solution

                  72 + 54 + 2744 = 2870 bits. Time = 2.87 ms.

                  Numerical 3

                  Address capacity

                  What does a 3-bit AM_ADDR give?

                  Solution

                  2³ = 8 values. 0 is broadcast, so 7 active slaves.

                  Numerical 4

                  Voice channels

                  Number of 64 kbps SCO links that would fit in a 721 kbps budget, ignoring protocol limits.

                  Solution

                  721/64 = 11.27, so 11 in pure arithmetic. In practice, slots and the standard limit SCO to 3 links, so state that.

                  7Solved scenarios

                  Scenario 6.8.1Built like your FAT10 marks

                  Fitness band with a phone

                  A band streams heart rate to a phone and a call is taken on the band. (a) Identify master/slave and links used for each traffic. 3 M (b) Explain the connection process. 3 M (c) Draw the mode tree and pick modes for idle periods. 4 M

                  Solution

                  (a) 3M Phone = master, band = slave. Heart rate is ACL (packet data, delivery matters). Call audio is SCO (real-time, no retransmission, 64 kbps).

                  (b) 3M Inquiry: phone discovers the band, which returns address and name. Paging: devices form the link. Connection: operating mode decided.

                  (c) 4M

                  Between heart-rate samples: Sniff, slave is free except for recurring slots. Longer one-off gap: Hold. Overnight: Park, wakes only when master says.

                  Scenario 6.8.2Built like your FAT10 marks

                  HC-05 phone-controlled lamp

                  A lamp on Arduino pin 7 is controlled from a phone over HC-05. (a) Draw the wiring block diagram. 3 M (b) Write the program. 5 M (c) Which stack layer makes HC-05 look like a serial port? State default settings. 2 M

                  Solution
                  Decode the question: "phone command" → Serial.read(). "turn on LED" → digitalWrite. "Bluetooth module" → UART link to HC-05.

                  (a) 3M

                  (b) 5M

                  #define ledPin 7
int state = 0;
void setup() {
  pinMode(ledPin, OUTPUT);
  digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);
  Serial.begin(9600);       // HC-05 default
}
void loop() {
  if (Serial.available() > 0) state = Serial.read();
  if (state == '0') { digitalWrite(ledPin, LOW);  Serial.println("LED: OFF"); state = 0; }
  else if (state == '1') { digitalWrite(ledPin, HIGH); Serial.println("LED: ON"); state = 0; }
}

                  (c) 2M RFCOMM emulates serial ports. HC-05 defaults: slave, 9600 baud, 8 data, 1 stop, no parity, PIN 1234.

                  8Tips & traps

                  Slide check: Baud: Slide 135's code uses Serial.begin(38400), while the HC-05's default data baud is 9600 (38400 is its AT-mode rate). Write 9600 unless the question gives a rate.
                  Slide check: Class 3 range: Slides list 10 cm. Many references say about 1 m. Write the slide's figure.
                  MODULE 6 · UNIT 9

                  Wi-Fi

                  Designing wireless networks, exactly how your FAT asked it.

                  PYQ: Q7 (10 M)Open designAP calculations
                  How it comes in the exam

                  Q7 was a Wi-Fi office design, 5+5. This is an open design answer. A fixed checklist and a device calculation separate top marks from average ones.

                  Your path through this unit

                  Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

                    1Learn it, step by step

                    Lesson 1

                    Wi-Fi basics

                    In plain words

                    An Access Point is the Wi-Fi equivalent of a post office: everything in the area goes through it. The SSID is the network name you see on your phone, and WPA is the lock on the door.

                    Write this in the exam
                    • Wi-Fi refers to the IEEE 802.11 standard for WLANs. Uses radio, in unlicensed spectrum.
                    • Elements: Access Point, Wi-Fi cards, safeguards (firewalls, anti-virus).
                    • SSID: 32-character network name. WPA, WPA2, WPA3: secure the network.

                    Remember: AP = base station · SSID = name · WPA = lock.

                    Check yourself: What's an SSID?

                    The name that identifies a Wi-Fi network, up to 32 characters.

                    Lesson 2

                    Two topologies and AP limits

                    In plain words

                    Ad-hoc is walkie-talkies: devices talk directly. Infrastructure is a telephone exchange: all calls go via the AP. Offices always use infrastructure.

                    The slide figure to remember for design is about 30 users per AP.

                    Write this in the exam
                    • Peer-to-peer: AP not required, quick to set up, clients communicate directly.
                    • Infrastructure: any communication goes through the AP.
                    • A single AP supports up to 30 users, 100–150 ft indoors, up to 300 ft outdoors.
                    • Many APs can be connected via Ethernet into one large network.
                    • Limitations: interference, degradation in performance, high power, limited range.

                    Remember: Devices ÷ 30 = minimum APs.

                    Check yourself: 90 devices need at least how many APs?

                    3.

                    Lesson 3

                    Designing a network: bands and channels

                    In plain words

                    The two bands trade range against speed. 2.4 GHz reaches further but is crowded. 5 GHz is faster but shorter range. Neighbouring APs on the same channel talk over each other, so give them different channels. In 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6, 11 don't overlap.

                    Write this in the exam
                    • Count devices, then APs = devices ÷ 30, then adjust for floors and rooms.
                    • Place APs centrally on the ceiling, away from metal, with slight cell overlap for roaming.
                    • 5 GHz for laptops and phones. 2.4 GHz for IoT and long range.
                    • 2.4 GHz channels: 1, 6, 11. Adjacent APs never share a channel.
                    • Separate VLAN/SSID for IoT and guests. WPA2/3-Enterprise.

                    Remember: Cats And Bats Chase Squirrels: Count, AP, Bands, Channels, Security.

                    Check yourself: Why put IoT devices on their own network?

                    Security isolation, and they don't compete with staff traffic.

                    Lesson 4

                    Handling peak traffic

                    In plain words

                    At 11 am everyone joins a video call. To keep things usable, spread clients across APs, let urgent traffic go first, and stop any single device from hogging the air.

                    Write this in the exam
                    • Load balancing across APs, with a cap on clients per AP.
                    • QoS (WMM): voice and video first.
                    • Band steering of dual-band clients to 5 GHz.
                    • Rate and airtime limits. Gigabit wired backhaul.
                    • Monitor utilisation, and add APs at hot spots.

                    Remember: Lazy Queues Bring Real Misery: Load, QoS, Band, Rate, Monitor.

                    Check yourself: What does band steering do?

                    It moves dual-band clients to 5 GHz, leaving 2.4 GHz for devices that need it.

                    Final step

                    Practice on paper

                    Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 6.9.1, Scenario 6.9.2 as you would in the exam. Then do the 4 numericals. Then try your own numbers in the labs.

                    2Memorise sheet

                    • Elements: Access Point, Wi-Fi cards, safeguards (firewall). SSID up to 32 chars. WPA/WPA2/WPA3.
                    • Topologies: Peer-to-peer (Ad-hoc, no AP), Infrastructure (via AP).
                    • AP capacity per slide: about 30 users, 100–150 ft indoors, 300 ft outdoors. APs join via Ethernet into one network.
                    • Advantages: mobility, installation, flexibility, roaming, speed. Limits: interference, degradation, high power, limited range.

                    Part (a): design
                    Cats And Bats Chase Squirrels = Count devices, AP placement, Bands, Channels, Security.
                    Part (b): peak load

                    4Diagrams & symbol checklist

                    Tick each symbol once you can draw it from memory.

                    5Keyword → function → diagram

                    KeywordMaps toDiagram
                    "multiple floors"AP per floor, staggeredFloor stack
                    "conference rooms"Dedicated AP thereExtra AP mark

                    6Numericals

                    Numerical 1

                    AP count for 50 staff

                    50 staff with a laptop and a phone each, plus 20 IoT devices.

                    Solution

                    Devices = 100 + 20 = 120. 120/30 = 4 APs minimum. Add for floors and rooms: 6 to 8.

                    Numerical 2

                    Shared airtime

                    An AP at 300 Mb/s real throughput with 30 active users.

                    Solution

                    300/30 = 10 Mb/s each, on average.

                    Numerical 3

                    Channel reuse

                    3 APs on one 2.4 GHz floor. Assign channels.

                    Solution

                    Use 1, 6, 11 so none overlap. Adjacent APs always get different channels.

                    Numerical 4

                    Coverage in feet

                    A 150 ft × 100 ft floor, with an AP reliable to a 50 ft radius.

                    Solution

                    Each AP covers about 100 ft × 100 ft of usable square. 150/100 → 2 APs per floor for coverage, then check against the capacity count.

                    7Solved PYQ scenarios

                    Scenario 6.9.1PYQ Q710 marks

                    Wi-Fi for a 50-person multi-floor office

                    Set up Wi-Fi for around 50 employees, multiple floors and conference rooms, supporting laptops, smartphones and IoT such as smart printers and security cameras. (a) Design an efficient network, considering AP placement, frequency bands and channel selection. 5 M (b) How would you handle high traffic in peak usage while keeping performance for all? 5 M

                    Solution
                    Decode the question: Part (a) → run CABCS. Part (b) → run LQBRM. Show the number: devices ÷ 30.

                    (a) Design 5M

                    1. Count: 50 × 2 + about 20 IoT = 120 devices. At about 30 per AP → at least 4 APs. For 3 floors, plan 6–8 APs.
                    2. AP placement: ceiling mounted, central, away from metal and lifts, one in each conference room area, with cells overlapping about 15–20 % for roaming. Stagger APs between floors.
                    3. Bands: 5 GHz for laptops and phones (speed, less interference). 2.4 GHz for IoT, printers and cameras (range).
                    4. Channels: 2.4 GHz only 1, 6, 11. 5 GHz: 36, 40, 44, 48, 149… Neighbours never share, including floors above and below.
                    5. Infrastructure and security: APs wired by Ethernet to PoE switches, gigabit uplink. WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise for staff, guest SSID, and a separate IoT VLAN.

                    (b) Peak load 5M

                    1. Load balancing: a controller shifts clients off crowded APs and caps each AP's associations.
                    2. QoS (WMM): voice/video first, background data last. Cameras get a reserved rate.
                    3. Band steering: push dual-band clients to 5 GHz, leaving 2.4 GHz for IoT.
                    4. Rate limits: per-user limits and application limits on guest and updates. Minimum data rate to stop slow clients from hogging airtime.
                    5. Monitor and grow: watch utilisation, add APs at hot spots, gigabit backhaul avoids a wired bottleneck.
                    Scenario 6.9.2Built like your FAT10 marks

                    IoT cameras flooding a warehouse Wi-Fi

                    Six Wi-Fi cameras (4 Mb/s each) and 40 handheld scanners share a warehouse AP. Scanners keep timing out. (a) Diagnose, with numbers. 4 M (b) Fix it. 4 M (c) Compare Ad-hoc and Infrastructure modes for this site. 2 M

                    Solution

                    (a) 4M Devices = 46, above the 30-per-AP guide. Cameras add 6 × 4 = 24 Mb/s continuous, and they hold airtime. On shared 2.4 GHz, interference and contention cause time-outs for the small scanner packets.

                    (b) 4M Add a second AP. Move cameras to their own 5 GHz SSID and VLAN, or wire them with Ethernet. Scanners stay on channel 1 and 6 APs. Apply QoS favouring scanners.

                    (c) 2M Ad-hoc has no AP and is direct, quick but unmanaged. Infrastructure routes via AP, giving control, roaming and internet access, so choose infrastructure.

                    8Tips & traps

                    Tip: The number line "120 devices ÷ 30 per AP" is what makes your answer look engineered. It uses your own slide's figure.
                    Trap: Don't assign 2.4 GHz channels 1, 2, 3. They overlap. Only 1, 6, 11 are clear.
                    MODULE 7 · UNIT 1

                    Agriculture + Automotive

                    One method for any "You are designing…" question, shown on farms and cars.

                    Block diagramsHard real-time reasoning
                    How it comes in the exam

                    Module 7 is the home of "You are designing a…" questions, like Q3 (camera). The slides are mostly block diagrams, so the marks come from drawing the right blocks and explaining the loop.

                    Your path through this unit

                    Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

                      1Learn it, step by step

                      Lesson 1

                      What an embedded system is, and the 5-block method

                      In plain words

                      An embedded system is a computer hidden inside a product and built for one job. Almost every application has the same skeleton: it senses something, decides, then acts, and often tells someone. Learn this skeleton, and any device becomes a question you can answer.

                      Write this in the exam
                      • Embedded system: a special-purpose computer designed to perform dedicated functions with limited resources.
                      • Sectors: agricultural, automotive, consumer, industrial, medical.
                      • Design blocks: Sensors, Processor, Communication, Actuators, Display/power.
                      • Control loop: Sense → Decide → Act → Report.

                      Remember: Smart People Can Always Design: S-P-C-A-D.

                      Check yourself: Apply S-P-C-A-D to a smart fan.

                      S: temperature sensor. P: MCU. C: Bluetooth. A: PWM motor drive. D: LED display.

                      Lesson 2

                      Smart irrigation

                      In plain words

                      A simple loop: when the soil is dry, the pump turns on. Add a screen for the field and the cloud for the farmer's phone, and you have the whole slide design.

                      Write this in the exam
                      • Soil moisture, temperature and humidity sensors feed the embedded board.
                      • Relay drives the pump. 16×2 LCD through an I²C module. Cloud (ThingSpeak) for remote users.
                      • Benefits: resource optimisation, production, sustainability, cost saving, data-driven decisions, remote monitoring.
                      • Future: AI/ML, robotics, 5G, blockchain, automation in packing and logistics.

                      Remember: Two thresholds stop the pump chattering.

                      Check yourself: Why use two thresholds?

                      With one, readings near it switch the relay on and off rapidly.

                      Lesson 3

                      ABS: don't let the wheel lock

                      In plain words

                      A locked wheel skids, and the driver can't steer. ABS watches every wheel. If one is about to lock, it eases that brake off and reapplies it, many times a second.

                      Write this in the exam
                      • Components: wheel speed sensors, ECBM, master cylinder, brake light switch, valve block and pump, instrument panel.
                      • Operation: compute wheel slip; on impending lock, hold → release → reapply pressure.
                      • Hard real-time, over a robust bus such as CAN.

                      Remember: Hold → Release → Reapply.

                      Check yourself: What does ABS preserve besides stopping distance?

                      Steering control.

                      Lesson 4

                      Airbag and cruise control

                      In plain words

                      An airbag is a one-shot decision made in milliseconds. Cruise control is the opposite: a continuous, gentle loop that keeps adjusting the speed.

                      Write this in the exam
                      • Airbag: seat, weight, occupant, impact sensors → input devices → airbag MCU + F-RAM → inflator. CAN to radar and engine.
                      • Cruise: radar and speed data → control → throttle and brake commands. HMI for settings.

                      Remember: Airbag: one-shot · cruise: closed loop.

                      Check yourself: Why does an airbag need occupant sensors?

                      To avoid firing on an empty seat, and to adapt to the occupant.

                      Final step

                      Practice on paper

                      Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 7.1.1, Scenario 7.1.2, Scenario 7.1.3 as you would in the exam.

                      2Memorise sheet

                      • Embedded system: special-purpose computer with dedicated HW and SW and limited resources.
                      • Five sectors: agricultural, automotive, consumer, industrial, medical.
                      • Smart irrigation: soil moisture + temperature/humidity sensors → board → relay + pump, LCD on I²C, cloud (ThingSpeak) for remote users.
                      • Farm benefits: resource optimisation, more production, sustainability, cost saving, data-driven decisions, remote control. Trends: AI/ML, autonomous robots, 5G, blockchain, automated packing.
                      • Farm robot: LiDAR/depth camera/laser sensor (perception) + drive + arm actuator + control (PID, fuzzy, neural, nonlinear).
                      • ABS: wheel speed sensors, ECBM, master cylinder, brake light switch, modulator valves and pump. Stops wheel lock so the driver can steer.
                      • Airbag: seat position, weight, occupant, impact sensors → input devices → airbag MCU + F-RAM → inflator; CAN to radar/pretension and engine.
                      • Cruise control: radar + speed sensing → control → throttle and brake commands; HMI for setting.

                      Tick each symbol once you can draw it from memory.

                      "turn on pump"Relay + driverGPIO

                      "farmer checks on phone"Cloud via Wi-FiESP8266, UART

                      6Solved scenarios

                      Scenario 7.1.1Built like your FAT10 marks

                      Smart irrigation with remote monitoring

                      Design a low-cost smart irrigation controller which waters when soil is dry, displays moisture locally and lets the farmer see data on a phone. (a) Draw the block diagram naming each interface. 5 M (b) Explain the control logic, avoiding pump chatter. 3 M (c) State two benefits. 2 M

                      Solution
                      Decode the question: Nouns: soil, display, phone, pump → blocks. Verbs: waters → relay; displays → I²C; see on phone → Wi-Fi + cloud.

                      (a) 5M

                      (b) 3M Read moisture periodically. Use two thresholds for hysteresis: pump ON below 30 %, OFF above 50 %. Check the tank is not empty before running. Upload readings every interval. The gap between thresholds stops rapid relay chatter.

                      (c) 2M Saves water by watering only when needed. Reduces manual labour through remote monitoring.

                      Scenario 7.1.2Built like your FAT10 marks

                      Designing ABS for a car

                      Design an anti-lock braking system. (a) Draw the system and identify the sensors, controller and actuators. 4 M (b) Explain the working during hard braking. 4 M (c) Why must this be a hard real-time system, and which bus suits it? 2 M

                      Solution

                      (a) 4M

                      (b) 4M On hard braking, the ECU computes each wheel's slip from wheel speed vs. vehicle speed. If a wheel decelerates too quickly and is about to lock, the valve holds then releases pressure on that wheel. When it spins up, the pump reapplies pressure. The cycle repeats many times a second, keeping wheels near peak grip and allowing steering.

                      (c) 2M A late valve command causes lock-up, a safety failure, so deadlines are hard. CAN: robust to EMI, prioritised, with error detection.

                      Scenario 7.1.3Built like your FAT10 marks

                      Airbag deployment

                      (a) Draw the airbag controller block diagram. 4 M (b) Explain the sequence from impact to inflation. 3 M (c) Why F-RAM, and why use occupant sensors? 3 M

                      Solution

                      (a) 4M

                      (b) 3M Crash sensor signal reaches the MCU, which confirms a true crash against thresholds and combines occupant data. It fires the inflator. Gas (nitrogen) fills the bag in milliseconds.

                      (c) 3M F-RAM writes fast and non-volatile, so crash data is captured even if power is lost at impact. Occupant, weight and seat sensors stop deployment on an empty seat and adjust for a small occupant.

                      7Tips & traps

                      Tip: Add a watchdog and fail-safe line in safety systems: it earns credit and links to Q9.
                      Trap: Don't draw a pretty picture of a car. Your slides have those, but marks come from labelled blocks, arrows and interfaces.

                      Consumer, Industry, Medical

                      Same method for appliances, robots, medical devices and your FAT's camera.

                      PYQ: Q3 (10 M)Architecture + analysis
                      How it comes in the exam

                      Q3 asked for a digital camera architecture. It is not explicitly in your slides, but it uses the same block-diagram approach as the projector and hearing aid. Next time it could be any device.

                      Your path through this unit

                      Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

                        1Learn it, step by step

                        Lesson 1

                        Washing machine and industrial systems

                        In plain words

                        Splitting a job across two chips is common. One handles the screen. The other runs the motor precisely, so a busy display never makes the drum jerk.

                        Write this in the exam
                        • Washer: HMI MCU linked by UART to a motor-control MCU, with ADC sensors and PWM drivers.
                        • Machine control: manufacturing, robotics, energy management.
                        • Machine monitoring: predictive maintenance, quality control, fault detection and safety.

                        Remember: Separate the fast control from the slow UI.

                        Check yourself: Why PWM to the motor?

                        It controls the delivered power, and so speed, efficiently.

                        Lesson 2

                        Medical: hearing aid and defibrillator

                        In plain words

                        Medical devices tend to be a signal chain: pick up a tiny signal, clean it, digitise it, process it, and output a response. Battery life is everything, because some are implanted.

                        Write this in the exam
                        • Hearing aid: mic → preamp → A/D → DSP → D/A → speaker amp. Battery + power management.
                        • ICD: sensor → band-pass filter → ΣΔ ADC → bio-processor → actuator.
                        • Constraints: ultra-low power, hard real-time, high reliability.

                        Remember: Mice Ate Delicious Dessert Slowly: Mic, A/D, DSP, D/A, Speaker.

                        Check yourself: Why is the ICD hard real-time?

                        A late shock can be fatal.

                        Lesson 3

                        Camera architecture (your FAT Q3)

                        In plain words

                        Light enters and becomes numbers. The numbers become a picture, and the picture is saved. Sensors can read faster than cards can write, so a memory buffer sits in between. That's how burst shooting works.

                        Write this in the exam
                        • Lens + aperture focus light and set its amount. CMOS sensor converts light to charge.
                        • ADC digitises. ISP does demosaic, white balance, noise reduction. MCU handles AE, AF and UI.
                        • DRAM buffer absorbs bursts. Storage: fast SD, in RAW and JPEG.

                        Remember: Lions Stalk At Pond By Sunset: Lens, Sensor, ADC, Processor, Buffer, Storage.

                        Check yourself: What does the buffer do for action shots?

                        It holds burst frames faster than the card can write them.

                        Lesson 4

                        Resolution, ISO and dynamic range

                        In plain words

                        Three settings pull against each other. More pixels means more detail, but each pixel catches less light. Raising ISO brightens the image but also the noise. Dynamic range is how much of the brightest and darkest detail you can hold in one shot.

                        Write this in the exam
                        • Resolution: detail and cropping, but smaller pixels and more data.
                        • ISO: low in sun (clean), high at night (noisy, needs denoising).
                        • Dynamic range: keeps highlights and shadows. Use high-bit ADC and HDR.
                        • Conclusion: large sensor, moderate resolution, 14-bit ADC, fast buffer.

                        Remember: ISO up → brighter, noisier.

                        Check yourself: Why does an action shot at dusk need a high ISO?

                        The fast shutter admits little light, so gain must make up for it.

                        Lesson 5

                        Projector: the slide's full design example

                        In plain words

                        The module ends by designing a projector around a single powerful chip (SoC). Everything else is an input, an output, memory or power. It's the 5-block method again.

                        Write this in the exam
                        • SoC processor with SDRAM. Inputs: HDMI, VGA, audio/video interface.
                        • Outputs: speakers, backlight/light engine. Control: remote, keypads, MCU with I²C/SPI, temperature sensor.
                        • Power: AC-DC controllers. Storage and comms: Ethernet, USB, SD.

                        Remember: Everything hangs off the SoC.

                        Check yourself: Why is a temperature sensor in a projector?

                        The lamp runs hot, so the fan and shut-off need monitoring.

                        Final step

                        Practice on paper

                        Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario 7.2.1, Scenario 7.2.2, Scenario 7.2.3 as you would in the exam.

                        • Washing machine: water level, temperature, load, quality sensors. HMI MCU over UART to a motor control MCU. PWM to motor/pump drivers, heater, valves.
                        • Industry: machine control (manufacturing, robotics, energy) and machine monitoring (predictive maintenance, quality, fault detection and safety).
                        • Industrial robots: controller, force/torque sensor, operator interface, TCP/IP.
                        • Medical: vital sign monitor, BP, pulse oximeter, insulin pump, hearing aid, pacemaker.

                        • ICD: sensor → band-pass filter → ΣΔ ADC → bio-processor (preprocessing, velocity estimator, prescription) → actuator shock.
                        • Projector: SoC with SDRAM, HDMI/VGA inputs, audio, backlight/light engine, MCU, remote, keypads, temperature sensor.

                        Hearing aid

                        6Solved PYQ scenarios

                        Scenario 7.2.1PYQ Q310 marks

                        Wildlife action camera

                        Design a digital camera for wildlife photographers: capture high-speed action, from bright daylight to low-light forest. (a) Explain the architecture, covering lens, image sensor, processor, storage and other key components, and how they work together. 5 M (b) Analyse resolution, sensor sensitivity (ISO) and dynamic range. How do these affect performance across lighting scenarios? 5 M

                        Solution
                        Decode the question: "Architecture" + named components → draw L-S-A-P-B-S. "high-speed" → burst buffer. "Analyse… impact… scenarios" → table: factor × bright/shadow/night.

                        (a) Architecture 5M

                        • Lens + aperture: focus light and set its amount. Autofocus motor driven by the MCU.
                        • Image sensor (CMOS): converts light to charge per pixel. Back-illuminated for low light, global or fast rolling readout for motion.
                        • ADC: digitises pixels, 12–14 bit for tonal range.
                        • Processor (ISP/DSP + MCU): demosaic, white balance, noise reduction, autoexposure and autofocus. MCU handles buttons, LCD and timing.
                        • Buffer (DRAM): absorbs bursts because cards write slower than sensors read.
                        • Storage: fast SD/CFexpress, in RAW + JPEG.
                        • Others: LCD/viewfinder, battery + PMIC, buttons, IMU for stabilisation.

                        Together: shutter press → AE/AF lock → exposure → readout → ISP → buffer → card.

                        (b) Analysis 5M

                        FactorBright sunDeep shadowNight
                        ResolutionHigh detail, allows croppingSame detail, more noiseSmaller pixels hurt, favour larger pixels
                        ISOLow (100–400), cleanMedium, balance noiseHigh (3200+), noisy, needs denoise
                        Dynamic rangeMust hold sky highlightsMust lift dark furLimited by sensor noise floor

                        Trade-offs: higher resolution means smaller pixels, less light per pixel, more data per shot, fewer frames per second. Higher ISO allows the fast shutter that action needs but amplifies noise. High dynamic range (12–14 stops, HDR bracketing) preserves highlights and shadows in the same frame. So the design favours a large sensor with moderate resolution, 14-bit ADC, fast buffer and good denoising.

                        Scenario 7.2.2Built like your FAT10 marks

                        Implantable defibrillator

                        (a) Draw the ICD's signal chain. 4 M (b) Explain how it decides to deliver therapy. 3 M (c) Give three embedded design constraints with reasons. 3 M

                        Solution

                        (a) 4M

                        (b) 3M Heart signals are filtered and digitised. The bio-processor estimates activity and identifies dangerous rhythm. If confirmed, the prescription stage commands the actuator to deliver a shock through the coil.

                        (c) 3M Ultra-low power, since battery replacement needs surgery. Hard real-time, as delayed shock is fatal. High reliability, with self-test and a watchdog, as failure can't be tolerated.

                        Scenario 7.2.3Built like your FAT10 marks

                        Washing machine controller

                        Design a washing machine controller with touch UI and sensors for water level, temperature and load. (a) Block diagram. 4 M (b) Flow of one wash cycle as state sequence. 3 M (c) Justify separating HMI and motor MCUs. 3 M

                        Solution

                        (a) 4M

                        (b) 3M

                        Each transition is triggered by a sensor threshold or timer. Door open or imbalance goes to a safe stop.

                        (c) 3M The motor MCU runs time-critical PWM control and isn't disturbed by UI load. The HMI MCU handles display and graphics. UART keeps the link simple, and each can be updated separately.

                        7Tips & traps

                        Note: Camera isn't in your Module 7 slides, yet it came in the FAT. Be ready to apply S-P-C-A-D to any new device: drone, smartwatch, pulse oximeter, or projector.
                        Tip: A 5-mark "analyse" answer does best as a table. It's quick to write and shows comparison at a glance.
                        RTOS + THREADS · UNIT 1

                        eCos RTOS

                        A real-time OS you can trim down to just the parts you need.

                        Theory scenariosPriority inversion
                        How it comes in the exam

                        Theory-heavy, so question style is "explain + justify in scenario": configurability, ISR/DSR split, scheduler choice, and priority inversion.

                        Your path through this unit

                        Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

                          1Learn it, step by step

                          Lesson 1

                          What real-time means, and what eCos is

                          In plain words

                          A real-time system isn't necessarily fast. It's on time, always. A correct answer that arrives late counts as wrong, as with missile guidance or flight control.

                          eCos is an OS you assemble like Lego. Only pick the packages you need, and everything else isn't even compiled in, so the program stays small.

                          Write this in the exam
                          • Real-time system: correct output delivered late means a catastrophe.
                          • A real-time kernel guarantees task completion before a deadline. A normal kernel doesn't.
                          • eCos: open source tool to create embedded kernels and applications.
                          • Compile-time control through the C preprocessor reduces the application footprint.
                          • Components: HAL, real-time kernel, ISO C and math libraries, device drivers, GDB support. APIs: µITRON, POSIX, EL/IX, native.

                          Remember: Compile-time configuration = small footprint.

                          Check yourself: How does eCos reduce footprint?

                          Only the selected packages are built in, through compile-time configuration.

                          Lesson 2

                          HAL: same code on different chips

                          In plain words

                          Enabling interrupts takes different instructions on ARM and PowerPC. The HAL hides that. You always write the same macro, and the correct machine code is plugged in underneath.

                          Write this in the exam
                          • HAL: a software layer giving a platform-independent API for platform-specific functions. Enhances portability.
                          • Example: HAL_ENABLE_INTERRUPTS() is the same API on ARM and PowerPC, with different implementations.

                          Remember: Same macro, different assembly.

                          Check yourself: What must change when moving eCos code to a new CPU?

                          Only the HAL implementation. Application code stays the same.

                          Lesson 3

                          ISR and DSR: splitting up an interrupt

                          In plain words

                          Taking a phone call while driving: pull over, note the key fact, and deal with the rest later. The ISR is the quick note, and the DSR handles the rest. ISRs mustn't wait on anything, because the time they take must be bounded.

                          Write this in the exam
                          • VSR: array of pointers to exception handlers. Written in assembly. HAL_VSR_GET, HAL_VSR_SET.
                          • ISR: small and fast. Synchronisation primitives are not allowed.
                          • DSR: additional processing. Sync calls are allowed but must not block.
                          • Enable interrupts at the start of the ISR, so higher-priority interrupts can pre-empt and the system stays predictable.

                          Remember: ISR = fast, no waiting · DSR = rest, never block.

                          Check yourself: Why are sync calls banned in an ISR?

                          They could make it wait or sleep, and ISRs must be fast and time-bounded.

                          Lesson 4

                          The two schedulers

                          In plain words

                          Multilevel queue: each priority level is a queue that can hold many threads, taking turns. Bitmap: one thread per priority, so the scheduler only finds the highest set bit, which is simple and quick.

                          Write this in the exam
                          • Multilevel queue: multiple threads at the same priority, pre-emption between levels, timeslicing within a level.
                          • Bitmap: single thread at each priority, pre-emption between levels, simple and efficient.

                          Remember: Many at a level → queue · one per level → bitmap.

                          Check yourself: Two threads need equal priority. Which scheduler?

                          Multilevel queue.

                          Lesson 5

                          Sync tools and priority inversion

                          In plain words

                          Say a junior holds the only key to a room, and a senior needs it. A middle-ranking person then keeps the junior busy, so the senior waits on someone who doesn't even need the room. That's priority inversion. The fix is to promote the junior temporarily, so they finish and hand back the key.

                          Write this in the exam
                          • Sync: mutexes, counting semaphores, condition variables, flags, message boxes, spinlocks (SMP).
                          • Priority ceiling: owner raised to a predefined value. Not elegant.
                          • Priority inheritance: owner raised to the highest priority of threads waiting. Synchronisation calls are costlier.
                          • API: cyg_mutex_lock(), cyg_semaphore_wait(), cyg_cond_wait().

                          Remember: Inherit = highest waiter · Ceiling = preset value.

                          Check yourself: Kernel semaphores in eCos are of what type?

                          Counting.

                          Final step

                          Practice on paper

                          Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario R.1.1, Scenario R.1.2 as you would in the exam.

                          2Memorise sheet

                          • Real-time: a correct answer delivered late means catastrophe. Real-time kernels guarantee completion before a deadline; normal kernels don't.
                          • eCos: open source, configurable. Compile-time control via C preprocessor. Select only needed packages, so footprint shrinks.
                          • Core components: HAL, real-time kernel, ISO C + math libraries, device drivers, GDB support.
                          • APIs: µITRON, POSIX, EL/IX, native.
                          • HAL: platform-independent API over platform-specific code. HAL_ENABLE_INTERRUPTS() is the same macro on ARM and PowerPC.
                          • Interrupts: ISR is small and fast. DSR does extra work. Sync calls are not allowed in ISR. They are allowed in DSR but it must not block.
                          • Exceptions: HAL + kernel (default) or application handling. VSR table holds handlers, in assembly. HAL_VSR_GET, HAL_VSR_SET.
                          • Kernel API returns no error codes. It uses assertions: CYG_FAIL, CYG_ASSERT, CYG_ASSERTC.
                          Multilevel queueBitmap
                          Threads per priorityManyOnly one
                          Pre-emption between levelsYesYes
                          Timeslicing in a levelYesNot applicable
                          Key benefitFlexibilitySimple, efficient
                          • Sync: mutex, semaphore (counting), condition variable, flags, message box, spinlock (SMP).
                          • Priority inversion fixes: Ceiling: raise owner to a preset value (not elegant). Inheritance: raise owner to highest waiter (costlier sync calls).

                          6Solved scenarios

                          Scenario R.1.1Built like your FAT10 marks

                          Priority inversion in a spacecraft controller

                          Low-priority logger L holds a mutex needed by high-priority attitude task H. Medium task M then runs for a long time. (a) Explain what goes wrong with a timeline. 4 M (b) Show how eCos solves it, comparing both protocols. 4 M (c) Write the API calls for protection. 2 M

                          Solution
                          Decode the question: "Low holds, high needs" → priority inversion. "solves" → ceiling vs inheritance table. "API" → cyg_mutex_*.

                          (a) 4M

                          H waits on a task of lower priority that doesn't even use the resource, so its deadline can be missed.

                          (b) 4M

                          Priority inheritancePriority ceiling
                          RuleOwner raised to highest waiterOwner raised to preset value
                          HereL runs at H's level; M can't pre-emptL runs at the ceiling at once
                          CostSync calls costlierNot elegant; needs design-time value

                          (c) 2M cyg_mutex_init(&m); cyg_mutex_set_protocol(&m, CYG_MUTEX_INHERIT); cyg_mutex_lock(&m); /* critical */ cyg_mutex_unlock(&m);

                          Scenario R.1.2Built like your FAT10 marks

                          Interrupt-heavy motor drive

                          A motor drive gets an encoder interrupt every 100 µs. Each must update position and occasionally wake a control thread. (a) Divide this between ISR and DSR. 4 M (b) Why are sync calls banned in ISRs? 2 M (c) Pick a scheduler and justify it. 2 M (d) Why enable interrupts at the start of the ISR? 2 M

                          Solution

                          (a) 4M ISR: read and acknowledge encoder, update position counter, request DSR. DSR: run control checks and cyg_semaphore_post() to wake the thread. Thread: full control computation.

                          (b) 2M ISRs must be fast and time-bounded. A sync call could make the task wait or sleep, which is unacceptable.

                          (c) 2M Bitmap, when each task has a unique priority: simple and efficient, so overhead is low. Multilevel queue only if several threads share a level.

                          (d) 2M Enabling at the end loses predictability. Enabling at the start lets higher-priority interrupts pre-empt.

                          RTOS + THREADS · UNIT 2

                          POSIX Threads

                          Several jobs in one program, and how to stop them from corrupting shared data.

                          Code + keyword mappingRace conditions
                          How it comes in the exam

                          Expect a code-tracing or code-writing scenario. This is where keyword → function name pays off most: read the scenario, then pick the correct pthread_* call.

                          Your path through this unit

                          Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

                            1Learn it, step by step

                            Lesson 1

                            Why use threads, and the shared memory model

                            In plain words

                            A thread is a separate worker inside one program. All workers share the same desk (global memory), and each also has a personal notebook (private data). Sharing is convenient, but it's also how they get in each other's way.

                            Write this in the exam
                            • Suited to: work that can run simultaneously, long I/O waits, uneven CPU use, asynchronous events, priorities.
                            • All threads access the same global, shared memory, and also have private data.
                            • Programmers are responsible for synchronising access to globally shared data.

                            Remember: Shared globals need protection.

                            Check yourself: Do two threads see the same global variable?

                            Yes, which is why access must be synchronised.

                            Lesson 2

                            Create, join, exit

                            In plain words

                            pthread_create is hiring a worker and giving them a job. pthread_join is waiting at the door until they finish. Without the join, main can end, and the worker is killed along with it.

                            Write this in the exam
                            • pthread_t tid; pthread_attr_t attr; set up the ID and attributes.
                            • pthread_attr_init(&attr); retrieves default attributes.
                            • pthread_create(&tid, &attr, runner, argv[1]); creates the thread.
                            • pthread_join(tid, NULL); waits for it to exit. pthread_exit(0); ends it.
                            • Compile: gcc -lpthread -o a prime.c.

                            Remember: I Can Jump Early: Init, Create, Join, Exit.

                            Check yourself: What's the third argument of pthread_create?

                            The function the thread runs.

                            Lesson 3

                            Race conditions and mutexes

                            In plain words

                            count++ looks like one step, but it's three: read, add, write. Two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, so one increment vanishes. A mutex is a bathroom key: only whoever holds it can enter.

                            Write this in the exam
                            • Thread-safeness: running multiple threads simultaneously without clobbering shared data or creating race conditions.
                            • Mutex: mutual exclusion. pthread_mutex_lock(&m); /* critical section */ pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
                            • Keep the critical section short.

                            Remember: Lock → touch shared data → unlock.

                            Check yourself: What's a race condition?

                            A result that depends on the unsynchronised timing of threads.

                            Lesson 4

                            Condition variables and the four API groups

                            In plain words

                            A mutex stops collisions. It doesn't say "wake me when the data's ready". A condition variable does: a thread sleeps, using no CPU, until another one signals it.

                            Write this in the exam
                            • API groups: thread management, mutexes, condition variables, synchronisation.
                            • while (!ready) pthread_cond_wait(&c, &m); releases the mutex while sleeping and re-locks on wake.
                            • pthread_cond_signal(&c) wakes one thread. pthread_cond_broadcast(&c) wakes all.

                            Remember: Lock, While-wait, work, Unlock.

                            Check yourself: Why use while rather than if?

                            A wake-up can be spurious, so the condition must be rechecked.

                            Final step

                            Practice on paper

                            Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario R.2.1, Scenario R.2.2, Scenario R.2.3 as you would in the exam.

                            2Memorise sheet

                            • Suited to work that can run simultaneously, long I/O waits, uneven CPU use, asynchronous events, and priorities.
                            • Shared memory model: all threads see global memory; each also has private data. The programmer must protect shared data.
                            • Thread-safeness: running threads simultaneously without clobbering data or creating race conditions.
                            • API is an ANSI/IEEE standard, but implementations vary.
                            • Four groups: thread management, mutexes, condition variables, synchronisation (read/write locks, barriers).
                            • Compile with gcc -lpthread -o a prime.c, run ./a 100.

                            3Mnemonics & templates

                            I Can Jump Early = attr_Init, Create, Join, Exit.
                            Condition wait
                            L W U: Lock, While(cond not true) wait, work, Unlock.
                            Template: The skeleton from your slides

#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
void *runner(void *param);

int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
  pthread_t tid;
  pthread_attr_t attr;
  pthread_attr_init(&attr);
  pthread_create(&tid, &attr, runner, argv[1]);
  pthread_join(tid, NULL);
  return 0;
}
void *runner(void *param) {
  /* work */
  pthread_exit(0);
}

while (!ready) pthread_cond_wait(&c, &m);

                            6Solved scenarios

                            Scenario R.2.1Built like your FAT10 marks

                            Prime finder from your slides

                            Write a POSIX program that takes N on the command line and prints primes from 2 to N in a separate thread. (a) Write the code. 6 M (b) Explain each thread call. 2 M (c) Give compile, run and output for N=20. 2 M

                            Solution

                            (a) 6M

                            #include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>
void *runner(void *param);
int main(int argc, char *argv[]) {
  if (argc < 2) { fprintf(stderr, "USAGE: ./a <n>\n"); exit(1); }
  if (atoi(argv[1]) < 2) { fprintf(stderr, "n must be >= 2\n"); exit(1); }
  pthread_t tid; pthread_attr_t attr;
  printf("Prime Numbers: ");
  pthread_attr_init(&attr);
  pthread_create(&tid, &attr, runner, argv[1]);
  pthread_join(tid, NULL);
  printf("\nComplete\n");
  return 0;
}
void *runner(void *param) {
  int i, j, upper = atoi(param);
  for (i = 2; i < upper; i++) {
    int trap = 0;
    for (j = 2; j < i; j++) {
      if (i % j == 0) { trap = 1; break; }
    }
    if (trap == 0) printf("[%d] ", i);
  }
  pthread_exit(0);
}

                            (b) 2M attr_init retrieves default attributes. create starts runner with argv[1]. join makes main wait. exit ends the thread.

                            (c) 2M gcc -lpthread -o a prime.c then ./a 20. Output: Prime Numbers: [2] [3] [5] [7] [11] [13] [17] [19].

                            Scenario R.2.2Built like your FAT10 marks

                            Race on a sensor count

                            Two threads each do 1000 increments of a global event count. The final total sometimes reads under 2000. (a) Explain why with an interleaving. 3 M (b) Fix it in code. 5 M (c) Define thread safety and what the programmer owns in the shared memory model. 2 M

                            Solution
                            Decode the question: "Global" + "two threads" → shared data. "sometimes" → race. Function → pthread_mutex_*.

                            (a) 3M count++ is load, add, store. T1 loads 5. T2 loads 5. Both store 6. One increment is lost.

                            (b) 5M

                            #include <pthread.h>
#include <stdio.h>
int count = 0;
pthread_mutex_t m = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
void *work(void *a) {
  for (int i = 0; i < 1000; i++) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
    count++;
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
  }
  pthread_exit(0);
}
int main(void) {
  pthread_t a, b;
  pthread_create(&a, NULL, work, NULL);
  pthread_create(&b, NULL, work, NULL);
  pthread_join(a, NULL);
  pthread_join(b, NULL);
  printf("%d\n", count);   // always 2000
  return 0;
}

                            (c) 2M Thread-safe code runs in several threads simultaneously without clobbering data or racing. All threads share global memory, so the programmer must synchronise access to it.

                            Scenario R.2.3Built like your FAT10 marks

                            Producer-consumer sensor buffer

                            A sensor thread produces readings and a logger thread must sleep until a reading is ready. (a) Which pthread tools and why? 3 M (b) Write both thread bodies. 5 M (c) Why while and not if around wait? 2 M

                            Solution

                            (a) 3M A mutex protects the shared buffer and a condition variable lets the logger sleep without busy waiting.

                            (b) 5M

                            int value, ready = 0;
pthread_mutex_t m = PTHREAD_MUTEX_INITIALIZER;
pthread_cond_t  c = PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER;
void *sensor(void *a) {
  while (1) {
    int v = read_sensor();
    pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
    value = v; ready = 1;
    pthread_cond_signal(&c);
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
  }
}
void *logger(void *a) {
  while (1) {
    pthread_mutex_lock(&m);
    while (!ready) pthread_cond_wait(&c, &m);
    log_value(value); ready = 0;
    pthread_mutex_unlock(&m);
  }
}

                            (c) 2M A wake-up can be spurious, or another thread may consume first. while rechecks the condition. cond_wait releases the mutex while sleeping and re-locks on waking.

                            7Tips & traps

                            Trap: pthread_create takes the function name and a void * argument. Don't call it as runner(argv[1]).
                            Tip: Label both the main and worker timeline in a fork-join sketch, even when not asked. It shows understanding quickly.
                            Slide check: Prime code: Your slide loops i < upper, so N itself is excluded. Sample output for 100 still looks right since 100 isn't prime. Use i <= upper if the question says "including N".
                            RTOS + THREADS · UNIT 3

                            Protothreads

                            Threads for tiny chips: two bytes of RAM each and no stack.

                            MacrosC-switch traceCompare models
                            How it comes in the exam

                            Distinctive and easy to score. Expect "compare with threads and events", "write using PT macros", or "show the expansion".

                            Your path through this unit

                            Read each lesson, answer its "Check yourself", then tick it.

                              1Learn it, step by step

                              Lesson 1

                              Why not ordinary threads?

                              In plain words

                              Every ordinary thread reserves its own stack, like every worker owning a whole filing cabinet. On a chip with 2 KB of RAM, you run out. Event-driven code uses a single stack but is messy to write. Protothreads get the best of both: one stack, and code that still reads top to bottom.

                              Write this in the exam
                              • Extremely lightweight, stackless threads that provide a blocking context on top of an event-driven system.
                              • Purpose: sequential flow without complex state machines or full multi-threading.
                              • Pure C, no longjmp, only 2 bytes of RAM per protothread, with or without an OS.
                              • Applications: memory-constrained systems, event-driven protocol stacks, deeply embedded systems, sensor nodes.

                              Remember: One stack, 2 bytes each.

                              Check yourself: How much RAM does one protothread take?

                              Two bytes.

                              Lesson 2

                              The macros

                              In plain words

                              Every protothread has the same shape: begin, wait, act, end. Waiting doesn't freeze the chip. The function simply returns and tries again next time it's called.

                              Write this in the exam
                              • PT_INIT(pt), PT_THREAD(name_args), PT_BEGIN(pt), PT_END(pt).
                              • PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, cond), PT_WAIT_WHILE(pt, cond).
                              • PT_WAIT_THREAD(pt, thread), PT_SPAWN(pt, child, thread).
                              • PT_RESTART(pt), PT_EXIT(pt), PT_YIELD(pt), PT_YIELD_UNTIL(pt, cond), PT_SCHEDULE(f).
                              • Returns: PT_WAITING 0, PT_YIELDED 1, PT_EXITED 2, PT_ENDED 3.

                              Remember: Begin, Wait, End.

                              Check yourself: How do you schedule a protothread?

                              By calling its function, from an event handler, an OS, or another protothread.

                              Lesson 3

                              How it works: the C-switch trick

                              In plain words

                              Here's the clever bit. Before returning, the function writes its current line number into pt->lc. Next call, a switch statement jumps straight to that case, even into the middle of a while loop, which C allows. A bookmark replaces a stack.

                              Write this in the exam
                              • struct pt { unsigned short lc; };
                              • PT_BEGIN → switch(pt->lc) { case 0:
                              • PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, c) → pt->lc = __LINE__; case __LINE__: if(!(c)) return 0;
                              • PT_END → } pt->lc = 0; return 2;

                              Remember: Saves a line number, not a stack.

                              Check yourself: Why don't local variables survive a wait?

                              The function really returns, so its stack frame is gone. Use static.

                              Lesson 4

                              Threads vs events vs protothreads

                              In plain words

                              Examiners love a three-way comparison, so keep this table in your head. Protothreads sit between the other two.

                              ThreadsEventsProtothreads
                              StackOne per threadOneOne
                              Code styleSequentialState machineSequential
                              Pre-emptionYesNoNo
                              LockingExplicitNone neededImplicit
                              RAM per taskHighLow2 bytes
                              Write this in the exam
                              • Protothreads are a new point in the design space between event-driven and multithreaded.
                              • Threads have explicit locking, protothreads have implicit locking.
                              • Limit: no pre-emption and no preserved locals.

                              Remember: Sits between events and threads.

                              Check yourself: Which model gives sequential code at the lowest RAM cost?

                              Protothreads.

                              Final step

                              Practice on paper

                              Turn on practice mode and write out Scenario R.3.1, Scenario R.3.2 as you would in the exam. Then do the 4 numericals.

                              2Memorise sheet

                              • Extremely lightweight, stackless threads giving a blocking context over an event-driven system.
                              • Purpose: sequential flow without complex state machines or full multithreading. Conditional blocking in C functions.
                              • Threads need per-thread stack. Events and protothreads need one stack.
                              • Features: pure C, no longjmp, only 2 bytes RAM per protothread, with or without OS.
                              • Uses: memory-constrained systems, event-driven protocol stacks, deep embedded, sensor nodes.
                              • Scheduled by calling its function, from an event handler, by the OS (Contiki), or by another protothread.
                              • Locking: threads = explicit, protothreads = implicit.
                              • Return values: PT_WAITING 0, PT_YIELDED 1, PT_EXITED 2, PT_ENDED 3.
                              • Implementation: pt->lc stores a line number. switch jumps back.

                              3Mnemonics & templates

                              Shape
                              B-W-E: PT_BEGIN, PT_WAIT_UNTIL, PT_END.
                              Why it's tiny
                              "Saves a line number, not a stack."
                              Template: Fixed shape
                              #include "pt.h"
static struct pt p;
static PT_THREAD(task(struct pt *pt)) {
  PT_BEGIN(pt);
  while (1) {
    PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, condition);
    /* action */
  }
  PT_END(pt);
}
int main(void) {
  PT_INIT(&p);
  while (1) { task(&p); /* update condition */ }
}

                              Tick each symbol once you can draw it from memory.

                              KeywordMacroDiagram

                              "wait until"PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, c)Loop-back diamond
                              "wait while busy"PT_WAIT_WHILE(pt, c)Inverse diamond

                              6Numericals

                              Numerical 1

                              RAM comparison

                              20 tasks. Threads need 200 bytes of stack each. Protothreads need 2 bytes each plus one shared 200-byte stack.

                              Solution

                              Threads = 20 × 200 = 4000 B. Protothreads = 20 × 2 + 200 = 240 B. Saving = 3760 B, about 94 %.

                              Numerical 2

                              Trace the counter example

                              PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, counter == 3), main does example(); counter++ starting at 0. When does it print?

                              Solution

                              Call with 0, 1, 2: blocked. Call with counter = 3: prints, sets counter = 0, loops, blocks again. So it prints on the 4th call, and main then increments to 1.

                              Numerical 3

                              Expand a wait at line 12

                              Expand PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, c); on line 12.

                              Solution

                              pt->lc = 12; case 12: if (!(c)) return 0;

                              Numerical 4

                              What's the return value?

                              What does a function return when blocked, and when finished by PT_END?

                              Solution

                              Blocked: PT_WAITING = 0. Finished: pt->lc = 0; return PT_ENDED = 3 in the library. Your slides' simplified expansion shows return 2 or return 1, so answer from the macro definitions given in the question.

                              7Solved scenarios

                              Scenario R.3.1Built like your FAT10 marks

                              Sensor node with 2 KB RAM

                              A wireless sensor node with 2 KB RAM must wait for radio-ready, send, wait for ACK, then sleep, for several protocol tasks. (a) Compare threads, event-driven code, and protothreads. 3 M (b) Write the sender. 5 M (c) State one limitation. 2 M

                              Solution
                              Decode the question: "2 KB" → stackless. "wait for…" (twice) → two PT_WAIT_UNTIL. Each wait becomes a diamond in the flowchart.

                              (a) 3M

                              ThreadsEventsProtothreads
                              StackOne eachOneOne
                              Code styleSequentialState machineSequential
                              RAM per taskHighLow2 bytes
                              Pre-emptionYesNoNo

                              (b) 5M

                              static struct pt tx_pt;
static PT_THREAD(sender(struct pt *pt)) {
  PT_BEGIN(pt);
  while (1) {
    PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, radio_ready());
    radio_send(packet);
    PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, ack_received() || timed_out());
    radio_sleep();
    PT_YIELD_UNTIL(pt, wake_timer_expired());
  }
  PT_END(pt);
}

                              (c) 2M Local variables don't survive a wait since no stack is saved, so use static. A switch inside the protothread can also clash with the macro's switch.

                              Scenario R.3.2Built like your FAT10 marks

                              Show how the macro works

                              For the counter example (wait until counter = 1000, print, reset): (a) Write it with macros. 3 M (b) Show the C-switch expansion assuming the wait is on line 12. 4 M (c) Explain how the function resumes on the next call. 3 M

                              Solution

                              (a) 3M

                              static int counter;
static struct pt example_pt;
static PT_THREAD(example(struct pt *pt)) {
  PT_BEGIN(pt);
  while (1) {
    PT_WAIT_UNTIL(pt, counter == 1000);
    printf("Threshold reached\n");
    counter = 0;
  }
  PT_END(pt);
}

                              (b) 4M

                              static char example(struct pt *pt) {
  switch (pt->lc) { case 0:
    while (1) {
      pt->lc = 12; case 12:
      if (!(counter == 1000)) return 0;
      printf("Threshold reached\n");
      counter = 0;
    }
  } pt->lc = 0; return 2;
}

                              (c) 3M On the first call lc = 0, execution enters at case 0. It sets lc = 12 and returns 0 if the condition is false. On the next call switch(pt->lc) jumps straight to case 12 inside the while loop, which is legal C, and retests. So the continuation is resumed using 2 bytes, not a saved stack.

                              8Tips & traps

                              Trap: Local variables are lost across a wait. Make them static. Examiners like this limitation.
                              Tip: The phrase "implicit locking, no pre-emption" also answers why protothreads rarely need mutexes.
